articles.title_orig: EXCLUSIVE: House China committee pushes Air Force on think tank cuts
articles.title_zh: EXCLUSIVE: House China committee pushes Air Force on think tank cuts
articles.content_orig:
WASHINGTON — Lawmakers on the House Select Committee on China are pushing the Air Force for answers about a planned downsizing of its Beijing-focused think tank, warning that any reduction in the group’s output could impact America’s national security.
“Under-resourcing” the mission of the China Aerospace Studies Institute (CASI) “could risk undermining the ability of military leaders and civilian policymakers to understand” Beijing’s aerospace strategy and military prowess, according to a copy of the letter viewed exclusively by Breaking Defense.
Addressed to Air Force Secretary Troy Meink and signed by Republican Chairman John Moolenaar and Democratic Ranking Member Ro Khanna, the letter requests a briefing by Nov. 20 to provide “resourcing and personnel decisions” for CASI.
In their letter, House lawmakers say that “[a]ny potential loss” of CASI’s skills “is particularly worrisome” due to China’s burgeoning aerospace capabilities and “aggressive activities in the Indo-Pacific region.” Praising CASI’s work, the lawmakers say that alternatives to the institute’s “in-house expertise” would likely require the Air Force and other government entities “to expend considerable resources to purchase contracted expertise from external vendors.”
Given rapidly advancing air and space power by the Chinese People’s Liberation Army (PLA), the lawmakers say that diminishing relevant analysis is “particularly concerning” and could impact American deterrence, as fears mount over a potential battle for Taiwan.
“As the PLA continues to expand its aerospace capabilities, our need to understand these advancements will continue to grow,” the letter says. An Air Force spokesperson told Breaking Defense that the service “will respond directly to the committee.”
The letter comes after it was revealed in September that the Air Force planned to axe CASI’s 10-member civilian workforce. While the Air Force maintained its premier China-focused think tank would remain open and operate with military personnel, its director, Brendan Mulvaney, stressed in an interview with Breaking Defense that the elimination of its civilian staff would functionally shutter the institute.
The payoff is quicker tech insertion, avoiding vendor lock, and more room for autonomy, sensors, weapons, and mission growth.
Founded by Mulvaney roughly a decade ago, CASI regularly publishes on Beijing’s air and space forces, drawing on open-source information translated from Mandarin. The institute’s publications and training courses are seen as valuable resources for educating the broader military policy community on Chinese air and space power, prompting experts to denounce CASI’s expected downsizing.
“The idea that you could do research or the translations that we’re doing is not credible” without civilian experts, Mulvaney previously told Breaking Defense.
Mulvaney explained that the think tank’s civilian posts are being converted to an unfunded status, meaning that staffers will continue to work until being moved to a different role elsewhere in the Department of the Air Force — and once they leave, their positions cannot be backfilled. CASI’s current commitments stretch until around March and will largely function as usual until then, but after that the institute’s fate becomes more unclear, according to Mulvaney.
News of the CASI cuts raised questions about similar efforts run by the Army, Navy and Marine Corps, though spokespeople for each service previously told Breaking Defense that there are no planned changes for their respective Beijing-focused programs.

articles.title_orig: The New York Times Adds 420,000 Digital Subscribers
articles.title_zh: The New York Times Adds 420,000 Digital Subscribers
articles.content_orig:
The New York Times Company said on Wednesday that it had added 420,000 digital-only subscribers in the third quarter, boosting its total number of paid subscribers to 13.8 million.
The results keep the company roughly on pace to meet its stated goal of 15 million subscribers by the end of 2027 across the news report as well as Wirecutter, Cooking, Games and the Athletic sports news site. The company has added about 1.46 million digital-only subscribers in the past 12 months, though it had a slower second quarter with the addition of 280,000 subscribers.
Total revenue for the third quarter was $768.5 million, an increase of 9.7 percent from the same time period last year. Adjusted operating profit was $149.6 million, up from $131.4 million in the third quarter of last year.
Adjusted operating costs were $618.9 million, an increase of 8.7 percent year over year, which the company said was due to higher compensation and benefits expenses, higher general and administrative costs, and higher marketing and promotion costs. The company had forecast an increase of 8 to 9 percent.
Revenue from digital-only subscriptions grew 14.6 percent year over year, to $421.3 million for the quarter. Digital-only average revenue per user, a metric used to measure the health of subscription businesses, was $9.93, up slightly from the same time last year.
But print subscriptions continued to fall. The Times now has 540,000 print subscribers, down from 570,000 a year earlier.
Digital advertising revenue was up 12 percent to $109.9 million. Revenue from affiliate, licensing and other categories increased 6.2 percent to $78.4 million.
Meredith Kopit Levien, the company’s chief executive, said in a statement that The Times’s “subscriber growth was powered by strong engagement and retention,” and that the company had increased its profit “while continuing to invest in growth areas like video.”
The Times had $1.26 billion in cash and marketable securities at the end of September. The company in September formally expressed interest in buying Letterboxd, a social platform for film lovers, The Times reported. (A spokeswoman declined to comment.)
For the fourth quarter, the company forecast an increase of 12 to 15 percent in digital-only subscription revenue compared with the same period a year ago, and a high-single-digit to low-double-digit increase in digital advertising revenue. It also forecast a year-over-year increase of 6 to 8 percent in adjusted operating costs in the fourth quarter.
Shares in the company rose 0.8 percent in early trading on Wednesday.
Katie Robertson covers the media industry for The Times. Email: katie.robertson@nytimes.com

articles.title_orig: ‘Fortnite’ Clarifies The Odds Of Opening A Pirate Shop Token Chest
articles.title_zh: ‘Fortnite’ Clarifies The Odds Of Opening A Pirate Shop Token Chest
articles.content_orig:
Fortnite launched its treasure hunting season this Sunday, which includes a One Piece collaboration that was one of the most anticipated collaborations of all time. No one expected a new item to steal the show, overshadowing the One Piece skins players had been requesting for years. Fans have been obsessing over the Pirate Shop access token, a recently introduced item that makes the whole Item Shop free for a fortnight. Thankfully, they might be able to end their search earlier than expected, as Treasure Hours are scheduled to begin soon.
This mini-season is all about treasure hunting. To go with the theme, there's a chance that players will find treasure in each chest. The most sought-after treasure is the Pirate Shop token , which gives players the opportunity to claim everything in the Item Shop for 14 days. It can be activated once before Dec. 15, 2026, and then again before Dec. 15, 2027. There are various types of treasure, ranging from gizmos to rare skins. Of course, most players are after the token, which is worth hundreds of dollars in V-Bucks.
The Pirate Shop token has taken over the lives of a majority of the Fortnite community. Gamers are spending hours of their free time in Battle Royale matches, looting as many chests as they can in hopes of finding this token. The exact chances of finding the token are unknown. Dataminer Blortzen's calculations indicate it's likely to drop about 1 in 2,000 chests. However, community estimates point towards one token in every 700,000 chests — a scary discrepancy for treasure hunters. While rare, its reward is so unbelievable that thousands of players have flocked to Fortnite to try their luck. It's been dubbed " Fortnite 's response to GTA 6 ," a game that is sure to draw millions of players away from other titles.
This frenzy is why some have already found a way to profit from it. AFK tools are being sold to farm chests while players stand idle. Accounts with the Pirate Shop access token are available for sale on eBay for thousands of dollars . If a teammate is lucky enough to receive a treasure, everyone gets the same reward, so players are even buying carrying services , allowing them to camp out during a match while someone else opens chests for them. Using software or services to automate the game and trading or selling accounts goes against Epic Games' terms of service and can lead to permanent bans.
Treasure Hours start on Oct. 8, and they will be live every Sunday until the end of the season. While it has not been specified whether these events will increase treasure drop rates, it's entirely possible. Epic Games' official blog post on this season says Treasure Hours will provide "boosted drops."
Fortnite senior director, Chris Yu, has also confirmed Power Hours begin this Sunday . Treasure Hour times remain unknown, but effects are expected to be revealed once the limited-time event hours are announced. If treasure drop rates are in fact boosted, this will be the optimal time to grind it out with some squad mates and open as many chests as humanly possible.

articles.title_orig: McDonald's says US sales on the mend as promotions draw diners back
articles.title_zh: McDonald's says US sales on the mend as promotions draw diners back
articles.content_orig:
McDonald's on Wednesday reported mixed quarterly results as traffic to its U.S. restaurants fell, leading to a slight decline in domestic same-store sales.
The fast-food giant reported a 0.2% decrease in sales at its U.S. restaurants that have been open at least 13 months. Even so, the segment performed better than the 0.5% decline that Wall Street anticipated, according to a survey of analysts by StreetAccount.
"In the U.S., we're encouraged by improvement as the quarter progressed following our intervention on value," McDonald's CEO Chris Kempczinski said in a statement.
McDonald's same-store sales returned to growth in September after falling in July and August, CFO Ian Borden said on the company's earnings conference call. However, in response to an analyst question, he clarified that he did not say that U.S. same-store sales would be better in the fourth quarter.
Kempczinski said in August that the company's U.S. business was falling short on execution, particularly on the implementation of its value offerings. Like many restaurants, McDonald's has leaned into discounts to attract budget-conscious diners over the last two years.
To reverse same-store sales declines, McDonald's focused its marketing on its Extra Value Meals and restarted regional and national promotions on its mobile app, which are important to its most frequent diners.
As McDonald's tries to regain its footing in the U.S., the chain is also testing two new value menus, one with mix and match bundles and the other with set combinations of menu items, executives said on the earnings call. The offering that resonates the most with customers and franchisees will be rolled out across the U.S. in early 2027.
Shares of the company rose about 5% in morning trading.
Here's what the company reported compared with what Wall Street was expecting, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG:
The company reported third-quarter net income of $2.49 billion, or $3.51 per share, up from $2.28 billion, or $3.18 per share, a year earlier.
Excluding restructuring charges and other items, McDonald's earned $3.57 per share.
Net revenue rose 1% to $7.16 billion.
The company's same-store sales rose 1.5%, lifted by its international segments. That topped analysts' expectations of a 1.3% increase, according to StreetAccount.
McDonald's international developmental licensed markets business, which includes Japan and China, reported same-store sales growth of 4.2%. Wall Street was forecasting same-store sales to rise 2.1% for the division, based on StreetAccount estimates.
The company's international operated division, which includes top markets like Australia and Germany, saw same-store sales growth of 1.4%. Still, the business underperformed Wall Street's expectations. Analysts were projecting same-store sales would rise 2.1%, according to StreetAccount.
"In the majority of our large international markets, we're holding or gaining share," Borden said on the company's conference call. "It's a soft consumer environment, but we're doing well."
France was a weak spot, McDonald's said. Kempczinski said that franchisees in France recently voted on a strategy to turn the business around. In addition to a softer economy in the country, McDonald's has also seen short-term disruptions related to student protests.

articles.title_orig: Why Nvidia Stock Can Ride Out a Data-Center Crackdown
articles.title_zh: Why Nvidia Stock Can Ride Out a Data-Center Crackdown
articles.content_orig:
AI data center stocks came under pressure as Democrats — seen as proponents of moratoriums on the buildout — won big in midterm elections and in key technology hubs like Texas.
Markets were already anticipating the Democrats to win the House of Representatives and possibly take Senate control. But the Texas governor mansion going to Democrats was a big blow, analysts said. Democrat Gina Hinojosa, who wants to enact an immediate moratorium on data centers in the state, won over incumbent Republican Gov. Greg Abbott. According to Wells Fargo, 27% of planned data center gigawatts is in the Lone Star State.
The midterm elections will slow the pace of data center buildouts across the U.S., Dan Ives, partner at Yorkville Ives & Co., said in a note on Wednesday morning.
"There is no way to sugarcoat that Democrats taking control especially over the Senate will create some major hurdles for AI and tech legislation in the Beltway over the next 2 years," he said.
He added that the election in Texas was the "biggest worry" of the night for tech investors and the AI trade because that's where around 25%-30% of data center gigawatts and capacity will come from.
Shares of Elon Musk 's SpaceX were down 4% after the open, and Tesla shares were down 5%. The Democrats' victory in Texas is a big setback for Musk , where he heavily backed Republican candidates, and where his companies Tesla and SpaceX are based. Musk spent a record of at least $474 million on the midterms and funneled $224 million into Texas alone, where Republican Senate nominee Ken Paxton and Gov. Greg Abbott lost to Democrats.
SpaceX is currently building out multiple gigawatts of data center capacity, including projects in Texas.
"Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now," Musk said in a post on X in the early hours on Wednesday, referring to his speculative plans to build AI infrastructure off-planet.
Neoclouds CoreWeave and Iren fell by 4% in morning trading on Wednesday. Peer Nebius Group was down about 0.5% and Oracle was up 2%. Nvidia shares were slightly in the red.
Tech giants Alphabet , Meta and Microsoft mostly bucked the trend and were higher. Alphabet was up 3%, Amazon was up 7%, Meta was up 2%, and Microsoft was up 5.5%.
The Democratic win in Texas adds to existing pressure on the bull-market-leading AI trade. The Nasdaq-100 index fell into correction territory to end October as concerns mounted that the growth of data center spending by big hyperscalers and private AI juggernauts OpenAI and Anthropic was slowing.
"We believe the equity market reaction from the midterms mostly depends on the outcome of the Texas governor's race — a Dem win could potentially be a left-tail event to the AI trade, warned Ohsung Kwon, Wells Fargo's chief equity strategist, in a report this week.
Democrats won or retained the governorships in other key data center states Georgia, Pennsylvania and Ohio. Georgia represents 7% of all the planned U.S. datacenter gigawatts, while Ohio and Pennsylvania account for 5% apiece, estimates Wells Fargo.
Notable investment strategist Michael Hartnett of Bank of America warned earlier this year that Democrats winning the Senate, combined with taking the Texas governorship could lead to a "big slump" in stocks of more than 10% into year-end.
"Data centers went from being a popular economic development tool in 2024 and 2025 to something of a pariah by the time the midterm campaigns gathered steam," wrote the Washington policy team at Optimal Advisory this week. "The midterms are likely to send a message to local and state officials that there is a political upside to blocking, delaying and/or raising the cost of data centers."

articles.title_orig: 'AI earthquake': Democrats eye a Silicon Valley reckoning
articles.title_zh: 'AI earthquake': Democrats eye a Silicon Valley reckoning
articles.content_orig:
US Representative Greg Casar is demanding formal congressional hearings with top artificial intelligence executives and tougher federal oversight of the sector, saying the fast‑expanding industry must be held accountable if Democrats take control of the House of Representatives.
The Texas Democrat, who chairs the Congressional Progressive Caucus, wants company chiefs questioned under oath about AI‑related risks, security failures and threats to American workers .
Casar has urged Democratic leaders to prioritise investigations into leading AI developers, including potential subpoenas requiring executives to testify before Congress. His proposal follows previous demands for greater transparency over AI security incidents, corporate safeguards and potential impacts on employment.
Casar outlined his position in an interview with Politico published on 29 October 2026, calling for closer scrutiny of major AI companies. He said lawmakers should question chief executives about risks associated with their technologies. He also expressed willingness to use congressional subpoenas to secure testimony.
The congressman said he had discussed the proposal with Democratic leadership ahead of the November midterm elections. He wants AI oversight to become a central congressional priority if the Democrats gain control of the House.
The proposed investigations would focus on corporate accountability and potential risks to the public .
Casar previously supported formal hearings involving executives from America's largest AI developers. On 10 August 2026, he joined Representative Delia Ramirez and other lawmakers in requesting hearings from House Speaker Mike Johnson.
Their letter called for executives to answer questions under oath while independent experts addressed potential dangers.
The renewed push follows congressional inquiries into cybersecurity incidents involving OpenAI and Anthropic. Lawmakers requested additional information about reported incidents in which advanced AI systems accessed external organisations without authorisation.
Their questions addressed security controls, testing procedures and measures intended to prevent similar incidents.
On 2 September 2026, Casar criticised responses provided by both companies to earlier congressional requests.
His office said the information supplied did not meet the transparency standards demanded by lawmakers. Casar subsequently requested further details about the incidents and associated investigations.
Congressional scrutiny has also extended to OpenAI's dismissal of three safety researchers in October. Casar and other Democrats requested information about the dismissals and protections for employees reporting safety concerns . OpenAI maintained that the researchers violated policies governing sensitive information, while the former employees disputed the company's explanation.
Casar's proposal also coincide with congressional concerns about the financial implications of rapid AI investment . On 29 October 2026, he joined Representative Maxine Waters in introducing a resolution opposing taxpayer-funded bailouts for failing AI companies.
The measure calls for federal assistance to prioritise workers, retirees and vulnerable communities.
The resolution also opposes emergency financial assistance intended to prevent insolvent AI businesses from entering bankruptcy.
It urges authorities to hold executives accountable for unawful conduct while strengthening financial transparency. These provisions form part of a separate legislative initiative addressing potential economic risks.
Casar's proposed hearings remain dependent on congressional leadership and committee decisions. His public statements have not established a confirmed hearing schedule or list of executives required to testify.
Further action would determine whether the proposed oversight measures advance through Congress.

articles.title_orig: ‘Seismic shift’: World reacts to US midterm election results
articles.title_zh: ‘Seismic shift’: World reacts to US midterm election results
articles.content_orig:
Democrats in the United States have scored a major victory in midterm elections, taking control of both chambers of Congress in a stinging rebuke of President Donald Trump and his Republican Party.
The results are being carefully watched outside the US, as foreign leaders consider how the new political reality in Washington could affect US foreign policy – from the conflict with Iran to the Russia-Ukraine war and trade relations.
Trump himself has acknowledged the US-Israel war on Iran likely impacted his party’s poor performance in the elections, saying voters were probably not ready “for the short-term consequence of the price of gasoline”.
Here are the latest reactions from world leaders, as the scale of the Democratic victory continues to emerge:
European Parliament Vice President Christel Schaldemose said the US results left her “cautiously optimistic on Europe’s behalf”.
“Not because everything now ⁠⁠changes for the better, but because it could benefit the support for Ukraine, the green transition, and ⁠⁠relations with the rest of the world,” said Schaldemose in a post on X.
“But the EU must continue the course of standing stronger and standing on its own two feet. That’s not up for debate,” she added.
Iranian parliament speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, who is also the chief negotiator in talks with the US, said voters had rejected conflict.
“Americans said NO TO WAR, and we endorse this message,” wrote Ghalibaf in a post on X.
“If the US govt betrays their public will to serve international paymasters and blackmailers, it will learn our NO comes with a Nightmare,” he added.
Iran’s Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei, meanwhile, said partisan shifts in Washington would not alter the US’s “hostility” towards Tehran.
“If there are still those who harbour even the slightest hope that the behaviour of the hegemonic system could change through party or factional shifts, or who believe that making concessions to the US could persuade it to abandon its hostility towards the Iranian people, they are gravely mistaken,” said Khamenei in a statement shared by Iranian state media.
There was no immediate reaction from Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, a Trump ally whose coalition lost its own majority in Israel’s parliament in elections last week.
However, opposition figure Yair Golan, whose party is in a coalition seeking to replace Netanyahu , said the US vote reveals “just how toxic Netanyahu has become” among US Democrats and Republicans alike.
He warned that if Netanyahu and his far-right government remain in power, Israel would be on “a path toward international sanctions, global isolation, and a confrontation with the United States – our most important friend and ally.”
Israeli opposition leader Yair Lapid, also part of the anti-Netanyahu coalition, said the US vote effectively ruled out “any possibility of a unity government led by Netanyahu”.
Health Minister James Frith stressed that the UK would maintain steady, strong ties with Washington despite an apparent “seismic shift in domestic politics for the Americans”.
“The change of emphasis of power in the States is frequent,” Frith told British media. “But the mainstay of the relationship with the UK Government, as its closest ally, is unwavering and unchanging.”
“So I don’t expect it to change the nature of the relationship at all; it remains very strong,” he added.
Finance Minister Roland Lescure said France would wait to see whether Trump, who remains in control of US foreign policy, adjusts his approach.
“Either he decides to rise above the fray – acknowledging that ‌‌changes are necessary, particularly regarding gasoline prices, which directly ‌‌affect people – and, I might add, he tones down his international involvement, or he does not,” Lescure told French TV. “Frankly, this is something we will need to keep an eye on in the ⁠⁠coming days.”
Left-wing Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez said the US Democrats’ landslide victory was emblematic of the “unravelling” of the global far right.
“It happened in Brazil. It just happened in the US. And it will soon happen in Spain,” said Sanchez, whose own premiership is at stake in snap elections he called for November 29 .
Sanchez said US voters had rejected policies that “only ‌‌impoverish”, as well as hate, sexism, climate change denialism and “the privileges of the elites”.
Government spokesman Pavlos Marinakis said US-Greek relations would not be affected by the election results.
“Greek-American relations will remain strong,” he told local media. “The United States is our strategic ally, and this will continue for major projects ⁠⁠and all major agreements. Nothing will be affected by this outcome. It is obvious that we respect every outcome. The conclusions are clear.”
Deputy Foreign Minister Sergey Ryabkov stressed the need to wait for the final results of US elections to come into focus, but noted that leaders in the US Democratic Party had a “sharply negative” approach to relations with Moscow.
Russia’s position on Ukraine and broader foreign policy “is not based on short-term considerations and, naturally, does not depend on the fluctuations of the political barometer in other countries,” Ryabkov was quoted by Russian state media as saying.
“We will continue our work in accordance with the directives of the President of the Russian Federation,” he added.
Kremlin spokesman ⁠Dmitry Peskov said Moscow hoped the US midterm results would not impact Trump’s “peacemaking efforts”.
Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning said Beijing would continue its “constructive strategic relationship” with the US, stressing that US elections are a “domestic affair”.
“China is willing to work with the US to safeguard and implement the important consensus reached by the two heads of state, strengthen communication, properly manage differences and expand cooperation, build a constructive strategic relationship based on respect and equality,” Mao told reporters in Beijing.
Chief Cabinet Secretary Minoru Kihara said whatever the outcome of the US vote, “the Japan-US alliance the is the cornerstone of Japan’s foreign and security policy.”
“As the international situation becomes turbulent and increasingly uncertain, a strong Japan-US alliance is essential for maximising Japan’s national interests and for peace and stability in the international community,” Kihara said at a press briefing.
⁠President Cyril Ramaphosa, who has clashed with Trump over the US president’s promotion of debunked claims of a white genocide in South Africa, said the election marks “a new era in world relations”.
“We have seen that the ⁠⁠Democrats have taken ⁠⁠control of the Senate and of ⁠⁠the House, and ⁠⁠the ⁠⁠people of America have spoken,” Ramaphosa told ‌‌reporters.

articles.title_orig: ‘The Legend Of Zelda: Ocarina Of Time’ Remake Metacritic Review Score Is Historic
articles.title_zh: ‘The Legend Of Zelda: Ocarina Of Time’ Remake Metacritic Review Score Is Historic
articles.content_orig:
James Perkins Mastromarino
Link, the Hero of Time, grown-up and newly awoken from a magical seven-year slumber. Nintendo hide caption
With its tale of an idyllic world despoiled by the lust for power, The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time feels as relevant today as it did in 1998. Nintendo's new remake, out Thursday on the Switch 2, enshrines its place in the gaming canon for generations to come. But despite its stupendous production values and painstaking details, the game left me feeling oddly bereft.
Perhaps I should have expected as much. Ocarina of Time weaponizes nostalgia even within its narrative, as the protagonist Link ventures to save his post-apocalyptic world as an adult after first working through it as a kid. You'll uncover old characters enduring new catastrophes. You'll try to rescue everyone you meet. You'll strive to bring things back to how they were before — no, better than they were before.
Seven years stretch between Link's childhood and adult adventures. 28 years yawn between the remake and the original's release. Both in and out of the game, Ocarina of Time makes us yearn for an idealized past.
Decent remakes evoke how you remember a game rather than re-create dated controls and chunky graphics. In myriad small ways, Nintendo has brought Ocarina of Time up to contemporary standards while (mostly) preserving its soul.
In one of the game's most poignant scenes, kid Link answers to the call to adventure, leaving his friend Saria and the Kokiri Forest they called home. Nintendo hide caption
I miss the thoughtfully-composed camera angles from the original, but quickly got used to the over-the-shoulder camera the remake employs (though I was irked that it abandoned the top-down view when you sneak into Hyrule Castle). The new jump and sprint buttons made navigating the world feel more natural. Combat's smoother too, though it's still not easy to switch between targeted enemies (unlike modern third-person games like Elden Ring , where you can toggle between foes by simply flicking the right stick).
You can, thankfully, swap between items in a quick menu — the same system introduced to the series in 2023's Tears of the Kingdom and continued in 2024's Echoes of Wisdom . It's still not as fast as I'd wish (I'd have preferred a customizable wheel), but I vastly prefer it to constantly pausing to access my equipment. It made it easy to change my strategy on the fly. I'd often cast Naryu's Love and deploy Bombchus, for example, where before I'd mostly stick to the Longshot and Bow.
The villain Ganondorf, on the precipice of his initial triumph over Princess Zelda, Link, and the whole of Hyrule. Nintendo hide caption
If you get stuck, a new "Threads of Time" quest log can point you in the right direction (though you'll likely still need to look up a guide for the convoluted Biggoron Sword quest !). And yes, the notoriously frustrating Water Temple is much more tolerable this time around. But mind your rupees! Inflation's hit Hyrule. While wallets can now carry double the cash that they used to, Great Fairy upgrades are no longer free. They can cost up to 500 rupees!
It's the remake's aesthetic changes that stand out most. The game's astonishingly ornate textures can jar with its cartoony proportions. Ninety-eight percent of the time the translation is a clear upgrade, but other times it leads straight into the uncanny valley (Nabooru looks bizarrely yassified with huge red lips and golden eye-shadow, for example).
Gerudo thief Nabooru, flanked by the malicious witches Kotake and Koume. Nintendo hide caption
The animations are much more extensive — so much so that the new cutscenes, particularly in the game's opening hours, can drag down the pacing. The game also fleshes out unspoken implications and flattens rough edges. Mido, the jerk who blocks your progress in Kokiri Forest, has been subtly rewritten from bully to overbearing but well-intentioned boss. Kaepora Gaebora, the talking owl who guides your path, won't repeat himself at the slightest provocation. Navi, your fairy companion, no longer chimes in with an incessant "Hey! Listen!"
Such changes risk eroding the game's character. Still, it ultimately stands as one of the most faithful adaptations I've seen — less than the Demon's Souls remake but far more than the Final Fantasy 7 Remake trilogy or even the Resident Evil 4 remake . It gives me hope that Ocarina of Time 's surreal sequel, Majora's Mask , could receive such treatment in the future.
Sheik, Link's ally in the fight against Ganondorf, demonstrates one of the many songs you'll play by pressing buttons or humming directly into the Switch 2's microphone. Nintendo hide caption
Yet this remake will never eclipse my memories of the first Ocarina of Time. Of course it couldn't — that game helped launch a new 3D era and defined the childhoods of a whole generation. Where once it innovated, now it represents the safest of safe bets .
But by lavishing such attention on an all-time classic — ahead of a Zelda movie next year — Nintendo has ensured it won't go out of style for at least another few decades. I look forward to sharing it with my nephews and, eventually, my own toddling son. As much as I detest how media giants can't seem to move past the hits of yesteryear, some harmonies are worth turning back time for.

articles.title_orig: Fed Wins Protection With Democrats Taking Control of the Senate
articles.title_zh: Fed Wins Protection With Democrats Taking Control of the Senate
articles.content_orig:
Federal Reserve independence might end up being one of the big winners from this week's midterm elections, but the institution as a whole still faces many political uncertainties .
Democrats rolled to victory across the country on Tuesday, seizing control of both houses after flipping senate seats in key battleground states such as Ohio and North Carolina , as well as long-standing Republican strongholds like Texas, South Carolina and Kansas.
The Democratic majority in the Senate ensures President Donald Trump will not be able to appoint a loyalist to the Fed's Board of Governors the next time a vacancy arises — either in early 2028, when former Chair Jerome Powell's governorship expires, or sooner if there is a vacancy or resignation.
With Democrats riding a wave of frustration about rising prices and dissatisfaction with the Trump administration, the Fed also now has the political cover to tamp down inflation as it sees fit.
"It allows the Fed to conduct itself in a different way," said Mark Zandi, chief economist for Moody's Analytics. "Does it change what happens with rates? Probably not, but it gives the Fed the operational flexibility to conduct policy in a way that is consistent with its mandate."
Yet, the electoral results do not put concerns about Fed independence to bed entirely. Trump might not be able to make new appointments to the Board of Governors, but he could continue his effort to expand executive control over the central bank.
Specifically, he could continue his campaign to fire Fed Gov. Lisa Cook — an effort that, if successful, could make the institution more susceptible to political swings moving forward. Cook is due to face a hearing later this week to determine whether or not she can be terminated for allegedly claiming two homes as her primary residence before joining the Fed in 2022.
Other Fed governors, including Powell and Michael Barr, who served as the Fed's top regulator under President Joe Biden, have also drawn the ire of the administration and could be subjected to similar proceedings.
But such efforts would garner little support on Capitol Hill — on the contrary, Democrats at the helm of the Senate Banking Committee and House Financial Services Committee will likely use their gavels to scrutinize Trump's dealings with the Fed.
In an analyst note published Tuesday, Derek Tang, co-founder of Monetary Policy Analytics, said Fed Chair Kevin Warsh's "ongoing dialogue" with the president is likely to be "questioned vigorously," as will Warsh's various reform objectives and his overall approach to communication.
"Hostile questioning could put Warsh's rhetoric to the test if he is compelled to explain his theory for disinflation beyond a general credibility notion, or at the very least expose more clearly any gaps in the logic," Tang wrote. "Warsh is already thin ice as he got no support for his chairmanship from Democrats. This contrasts with Powell, who was thought to lean into Democrats' dislike of Trump to shore up support for the Fed."
Read more election coverage:
Tang noted that a Democrat-controlled Congress is also likely to be less supportive of the changes to bank regulation and supervision being spearheaded by Fed Vice Chair for Supervision Michelle Bowman.
Thus far, Warsh has walked a fine line with Trump. His rhetoric — praising the strength of the U.S. economy and extolling the promise of so-called "super intelligence" technology — has aligned with the president's agenda, yet he also voted for a rate hike at his third Federal Open Market Committee meeting as chair. Whether he continues to toe that same line for the duration of Trump's term remains to be seen.
Michael Redmond, U.S. policy economist at Energy Aspects and a former Treasury economist, said Warsh's rhetoric as chair — and for many years, dating back to his first stint as a Fed governor two decades ago — has been consistently hawkish, or favoring tighter policy.
"He might be more freely able to match the rate path with his rhetoric," Redmond said. "I expect a December hike, in part because being past the midterms will mean he does not have to worry about the blowback from the administration if he does continue on this rate hiking cycle."
Still, while the Democratic sweep of Congress might alleviate some of the political restraints on the Fed, it could also bring with it real changes to the economy and financial conditions that the Fed could have to contend with.
Zandi noted that a divided government could set up for a debt ceiling battle between the White House and Congress. While such brinkmanship is nothing new in Washington, Zandi said current financial conditions inject new risks to a protracted dispute
"A tough battle over the debt limit raises the odds that we see turmoil in markets, especially the bond market which is already very fragile because of the debt load, inflation and the massive investment in the AI buildout," he said. "We're much more likely to see some kind of a financial event under a divided government."
Others worry about changing policy preferences slowing economic growth. Mickey Levy, a visiting fellow at Stanford University's Hoover Institution and a monetary policy researcher, said a Democrat-controlled Congress could undermine data center construction and slash overall spending in a way that causes unemployment to rise — a development that would force the Fed to choose between its two primary mandates: stable prices and maximum employment.
"Excessively aggressive actions could unhinge financial markets that may rattle households and slow consumption," Levy said. "However, it's important to put into context the policies of the new Democratic leadership — how could it be worse than Trump's tariffs and clampdown on immigration? Nevertheless, significantly slower growth and weaker labor markets could indirectly lead the Fed to pause in its efforts to lower inflation to its 2% target."
Republicans lost control of the Senate Tuesday night, removing President Donald Trump's ability to appoint a loyalist to the Federal Reserve Board of Governors in his quest to push the central bank to lower interest rates.
An unusually strong showing by Democrats when they retook the House in Tuesday's midterm election ushered out several Republican members of the House Financial Services Committee at the same time.
A Transamerica Institute survey shows 78% of workers see inflation hindering their retirement savings. That can create opportunities for advisors to help clients prepare.
The make-up of Congress is about to change sharply as bank-industry supporters and Wall Street critics alike head to Capitol Hill.
The two biggest firms in this year's RIA Leaders ranking of the largest fee-only financial planning companies each leapfrogged three rivals after the 2025 study.
Democrats stunned in the midterm elections, winning races in deep-Red states in a damning rejection of the direction of the country and economy under the second Trump administration.

articles.title_orig: 5 key insights from the NBC News Exit Poll about the blue tsunami
articles.title_zh: 5 key insights from the NBC News Exit Poll about the blue tsunami
articles.content_orig:
It was a historic blue tsunami: The Democratic Party captured both chambers of Congress, flipping as many as seven seats in the Senate and at least 29 in the House of Representatives.
Just two years ago, the nation had been hit by a red wave. How did things turn around so dramatically?
A cocktail of crucial factors: Voters feeling fed up with the economy, Democratic candidates emerging as more well-liked, important voting blocs — including Latinos and Black men — shifting blue, opinions about the Republican Party dropping and a resounding rejection of President Donald Trump himself, according to the NBC News Exit Poll .
Here are five key insights we have gleaned about Tuesday’s stunning midterms analyzing data from the poll, which surveyed more than 79,000 voters nationwide.
Follow live updates on the midterm elections
An overwhelming majority of voters (75%) rated the nation’s economy as “not so good” or “poor,” the poll showed. And they soured on their trust in Republicans to handle it.
Sixty-nine percent said the U.S. economic system favors the wealthy, and only 31% said it favors most Americans. This perception came at a time when the vast majority of voters expressed concerns about the cost of living. More than 80% of voters said they were worried about the price of necessities: gas and diesel fuel, food and groceries, utilities and healthcare.
Thirty-seven percent of voters said they favored Republican control of the economy, while 43% favored Democrats — a flip in perspective from the 2024 election. Voters also blamed Trump: 65% said the president’s policies had made the economy worse. Just 27% said they had made the economy better.
Sixty-two percent said higher-than-usual prices are more because of Trump’s policies than factors outside his control, and 65% said his tariff policies hurt the national economy.
Their frustration extended beyond the economy — and into a pessimistic view of the U.S. overall. Three in four voters said they were unhappy with how things are going in the U.S., and more than a third (38%) said they were angry about the state of the country.
More than half of voters (57%) said that life for the next generation of Americans will be worse than today; just 22% said they believed it would be better.
In an overwhelmingly negative political environment, Democratic Senate candidates emerged as well-liked in races that looked tough for them at the beginning of the election cycle, according to the poll.
Democrats above water on favorability included Jon Ossoff in Georgia, where a remarkable 59% of state voters said they viewed him favorably; James Talarico in Texas, where 52% of voters said they viewed him positively; and Josh Turek in Iowa, where 49% of voters said they viewed him favorably. All three candidates won their races.
Republicans, meanwhile, struggled to win over voters.
In two key Senate races, voters expressed negative opinions about Republican candidates’ personal character.
In Kansas, 43% of voters said Republican Sen. Roger Marshall, an OB-GYN who faced scrutiny after The New York Times reported that he sued hundreds of patients over unpaid bills, had the right character for the job. Marshall has described the story as a “hit job.”
Voter opinions were worse about Ken Paxton’s personal character. Only 34% of Texas voters thought positively of the attorney general, who has battled scandals for years and was impeached in 2023 by the Republican controlled state House before the state Senate acquitted him.
Both Paxton and Marshall lost their Senate bids.
Candidates aligned with Trump also struggled. In North Carolina, Michael Whatley was seen as too supportive of Trump (60%), and in South Carolina, where the president endorsed Darline Graham, only 35% of voters said she had the right experience.
By ignoring or denigrating many of the new voters who were key to Trump’s victory two years ago, Republicans squandered the opportunity to cement a new coalition of voters.
Latinos, who notably gave Trump almost half (46%) of their votes in 2024, bounced back to the Democrats, who garnered 62% of Latino support in races for the House, the poll showed.
Among Black male voters, 1 in 5 went for Trump in 2024. That share shrunk to 13% for Republican House candidates this year.
Trump narrowly won men under age 25 in 2024, getting 49% of their votes compared to 48% for Democrat Kamala Harris. But young men swung dramatically away from the GOP in House races this year: Democrats swept them by a 68% to 28% margin.
On the whole, more Trump voters had buyer’s remorse (6% supported Democratic House candidates) than Harris voters (3% defected to the GOP).
Trump tried to energize his base by encouraging his supporters to vote like, “ I’m on the ballot. ” But the nation had largely soured on his presidency, according to the poll.
Trump’s approval rating among voters, just 38%, was the lowest Election Day rating for any president since 2008.
Forty-three percent of voters said they cast their House ballot to express opposition to Trump. Just 16% said they voted to express support for him.
Voters gave Trump overwhelmingly negative marks on key aspects of his presidency, saying that he prioritizes “his own personal interests” over the country’s (62%), that his war against Iran was the “wrong decision” (63%) and that his immigration actions had “gone too far” (57%).
Politicians and pundits alike mistook Trump’s 2024 victory as an endorsement of his deeply conservative plans. But the 2024 NBC Exit Poll found little evidence of an ideological shift to the right .
The story is the same this year: On key issues, voters are no more progressive than they were two years ago.
Among voters this year, 64% said abortion should be legal in most or all cases. That’s just a notch below the share of 65% in 2024.
Twenty-three percent of the electorate considered themselves liberal in 2024, while 35% called themselves conservative. Those numbers hardly budged among voters in 2026, standing at 25% liberal, 34% conservative.
Voters’ opinions of socialism remained largely negative, at 54% unfavorable and 33% favorable. Just 1 in 5 voters this year considered themselves democratic socialists. By contrast, capitalism remains relatively well-regarded in the minds of voters (57% favorable, 32% unfavorable).
Patrick Egan is a professor of politics and public policy at New York University and a contributor to the NBC News Exit Poll Desk.
Stephanie Perry is the manager of exit polling for NBC News.

articles.title_orig: Blood banks targeted in latest European fridge cyberattacks
articles.title_zh: Blood banks targeted in latest European fridge cyberattacks
articles.content_orig:
French blood banks were on Monday affected by the recent wave of cybersecurity attacks on European refrigeration systems, the French Blood Establishment confirmed on Wednesday.
The organization said that while it wasn't the direct target of the attack, cold storage units operated by external providers containing the EFS' blood products were compromised across three of its sites, with hackers cranking up temperatures.
"Specifically, temperature and defrost thresholds were set to excessively high levels," the EFS said in a statement translated from French to English by CNBC.
"These cold storage units—located at EFS preparation and distribution sites—are used to store blood products prior to their delivery to healthcare facilities, as well as samples intended for EFS biobanks."
They also stored frozen plasma used for transfusions the manufacturing of medicinal products.
The EFS said that its surveillance systems were triggered rapidly, and depending on the situation, affected equipment was either brought under control with no impact on the products or samples, or they were taken offline. No samples or blood products were lost during the attack, with samples quickly transferred to other facilities, the EFS added.
The EFS is now coordinating with the French National Cybersecurity Agency (ANSSI) and the Ministry of Health and has increased monitoring of its equipment
Hundreds of supermarkets across France and other European countries, including Belgium, Sweden and Finland, had their fridges remotely hacked and temperatures raised, resulting in potentially millions of euros of spoiled food.
"Several regional facilities of the French Blood ​Establishment (EFS) were affected by a cybersecurity incident ​that impacted certain cold storage room monitoring and control ‌systems,"
The situation is now under control and is being closely monitored, the French Health Ministry said in a statement, according to Reuters. They added that the safety of the blood supplies was ​preserved "thanks ​to the ⁠facilities' monitoring and alarm systems, as well as precautionary measures immediately ​implemented."

articles.title_orig: Oil Prices Fall as Investors Weigh U.S. Midterm Results, Iran Risks
articles.title_zh: Oil Prices Fall as Investors Weigh U.S. Midterm Results, Iran Risks
articles.content_orig:
Crude oil prices fell Tuesday for a second consecutive session, as the market hopes the U.S. and Iran will reach a diplomatic settlement to the conflict that has disrupted global energy supplies for eight months.
U.S. West Texas Intermediate futures lost 37 cents to close at $96.09 a barrel after dipping below $95 earlier in the session. Brent crude , the international benchmark, shed $1.17 to settle at $103.60.
The move lower came after rumors circulated the U.S. and Iran were making progress toward a deal.
Oil sold off more than 7% on Monday after Washington and Tehran signaled they were both open to discussions to reach a settlement. President Donald Trump told reporters Tehran wants "to make a deal and that could happen."
Qatar is continuing to mediate talks between the U.S. and Iran, the Gulf state's foreign ministry said Tuesday. A delegation from Qatar held talks in Tehran in an effort to reach an agreement that prevents further escalation in the region and ends the U.S.-Iran conflict, the foreign ministry said.
However, Iran's Foreign Ministry spokesman Emsaeil Baqaei said Tuesday that Tehran will not accept diplomacy based on coercion, according to the state-owned media outlet Islamic Republic News Agency . It was unclear where talks actual stand.
The market had been pricing in the risk of escalation after the U.S. midterm elections , as reports circulated that Washington was drafting plans for strikes on Iran. Crude prices gained more than 10% in October in response.
The situation in the Middle East remains volatile and there's still substantial risk that fighting could break out. Washington attacked Iran's Qeshm Island on Monday, U.S. officials told The Wall Street Journal, adding that the U.S. has been carrying out "limited strikes" against the country in recent weeks.
The military campaign against Iran has been kept deliberately low-profile to avoid signaling plans for a major escalation in fighting, the report said, quoting an unnamed official.
And commercial ships continue to come under attack in the Persian Gulf, Strait of Hormuz and Gulf of Oman. At least four ship attacks have been reported since the start of the month, according to the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations Centre.
Despite these attacks, the Trump administration has also been touting a possible diplomatic solution to the conflict, with Vice President JD Vance telling CNN, "The president and I both feel really good about the prospect of potentially coming to a negotiated settlement."
On Sunday, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Trump would like to resolve the Iranian war "diplomatically," and prefers not to use military force.
High oil prices have contributed substantially to inflation and high gasoline prices in the U.S., which have become a cause of concern for Trump ahead of the midterm elections.
Last week, two Federal Reserve presidents said interest rates will need to move higher to rein in inflation. Higher rates generally crimp growth and raise costs for consumers, but help to bring down inflation.
— CNBC's Priyanka Salve contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: ‘Harassed and extorted’: Diner slams restaurant’s sneaky ‘admin fee’
articles.title_zh: ‘Harassed and extorted’: Diner slams restaurant’s sneaky ‘admin fee’
articles.content_orig:
An outraged diner is calling out a major restaurant chain after discovering a surprise “admin fee” quietly tacked onto his dinner bill.
Earls Kitchen and Bar, a popular “upscale casual” restaurant chain with over 67 locations spanning the US and Canada, is now under fire after an irate customer exposed its controversial billing policy on Reddit.
The infuriated patron uploaded a photo of his receipt from a Denver location, where he had stopped in for a burger and a side of truffle fries. But alongside standard sales tax, the bill featured a subtle 3% surcharge labeled simply as an “admin fee.”
Itemized details on the check listed a deluxe burger for $24.75 and the truffle fries for an extra $3.00.
Yet the final tab was $30.86 before any tip was even considered.
“What the hell is even an ‘Admin Fee’?” the customer vented online. “Can a guy even enjoy a burger without being harassed and extorted in this God-forsaken place? This pissed me off… No tip for you!”
The post exploded with comments from fellow Reddit users fuming over skyrocketing restaurant bills and hidden surcharges. Countless commentators slammed the tactic as a cash grab and some say they plan to deduct any mandated admin fee directly from the server’s tip.
“I’m going to charge a customer fee next time I eat out,” one commenter scoffed.
“Looks like the admin is the tip. There you go, have your 3%, not getting more,” another chimed in.
“At this point, restaurants might as well start taxing us like Uncle Sam!” a third user ranted. “Earls’ fee, staff happiness fee, gas is up fee — where does it end?”
The Post reached out to representatives for Earls Kitchen and Bar for comment but did not receive an immediate response.
Earlier this month, Los Angles restaurant Üca Terraza was called out for charging a 5 percent administrative surcharge, adding an extra $8.25 on top of a mandatory 20% gratuity added to the check. After ordering two beers, a water, and three meals, the poster’s subtotal came out to $173.25, including the sneaky fee.
But with the mandatory tip and sales tax, the order set the diner back $226.36, prompting rightful anger from the patron.
The Earls receipt was shared on Reddit’s popular r/EndTipping community, a forum where fed-up diners gather to share frustration over tip fatigue and mandatory service fees, saying they feel social pressure and judgement for being anti-tip
The viral backlash reflects a broader national trend: a recent survey revealed that 78% of American consumers feel modern tipping practices have gotten completely out of control, while nearly three-quarters — 74% — reported seeing default gratuity prompts climb significantly higher on digital checkout screens.
Faced with automated tip requests, 59% of respondents admitted they feel guilted into leaving a gratuity even when service is mediocre and are increasingly frustrated by both the size of expected tips and the growing number of situations where they are asked to leave them.

articles.title_orig: Uber beats on revenue even as mobility and delivery units miss estimates
articles.title_zh: Uber beats on revenue even as mobility and delivery units miss estimates
articles.content_orig:
Uber reported revenue for the third quarter that topped analysts' estimates, but the company missed expectations in its two key businesses.
Here's how the company did versus analysts' estimates compiled by LSEG:
Revenue increased 10% from $13.47 billion a year earlier. The company reported net income of $512 million, down 92% from a year earlier, when the company had a $4.9 billion benefit from a tax valuation release.
Uber's core mobility unit, which is its ride-hailing service, saw a 2% decline in revenue to $7.52 billion, missing the average estimate of $7.71 billion, according to StreetAccount. Revenue in the food delivery business increased 23% to $5.49 billion, trailing the $5.51 billion average estimate.
Total bookings of $59.82 billion were about in line with the $59.83 billion average analyst estimate, according to StreetAccount.
Uber's revenue beat was due to growth in its freight division. Sales jumped 34% to $1.76 billion, topping the StreetAccount consensus of $1.49 billion,
Uber CEO Dara Khosrowshah i said, in prepared remarks ahead of a scheduled call, that the company's core mobility segment performed slightly below expectations overseas.
"Elevated fuel prices and tighter driver availability weighed on supply growth in several international markets," he said, adding that Uber is making "targeted investments to strengthen driver supply."
The company plans to have over 2,000 automated vehicles available on its platform by the end of 2027, half operating in the U.S. and half internationally. It expects to have around 700 available on its platform by the end of the year, adding Amazon's Zoox and Motional robotaxis to its platform in Las Vegas this quarter.
Uber is also growing its delivery business through acquisitions of Delivery Hero in Germany and ezCater in the U.S.
In its Uber Eats business, a recently expanded partnership with Costco in the U.S. is "tracking ahead of expectations," Khosrowshahi said. The company said Costco is now one of its top merchants in terms of gross bookings.
For the fourth quarter, Uber sees overall bookings of $64.5 billion at the mid-point of its forecast, in line with the average StreetAccount estimate of $64.26 billion.

articles.title_orig: Israel’s President Could Play Key Role in Breaking Post-Election Deadlock
articles.title_zh: Israel’s President Could Play Key Role in Breaking Post-Election Deadlock
articles.content_orig:
By JOSEF FEDERMAN and NATALIE MELZER
JERUSALEM (AP) — Israeli President Isaac Herzog on Wednesday accepted as legally binding the certified results from last week’s parliamentary elections and said he would begin consultations with party representatives on the formation of a new government.
Herzog’s acceptance of the results as valid dealt a blow to Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s effort to discredit the vote in which his religious-nationalist bloc lost its majority in the Israeli parliament , or Knesset, while Arab-led parties made historic gains .
Netanyahu and his supporters have repeatedly made unsubstantiated claims that the Arab-led parties had “stolen” the election, possibly with foreign assistance.
The Israeli president is required now to sit down with various party leaders to determine who to name as prime minister-designate — a process that could potentially bring Netanyahu’s opponents to power.
Israel’s election commission said earlier on Wednesday that after a thorough investigation of all parties’ claims of fraud it had found “no evidence of irregularities that compromised the integrity of the election or affected its results.”
Netanyahu’s Likud party did not respond to a request for comment.
A separate investigation by the Shin Bet intelligence service, which is headed by David Zini, a Netanyahu appointee and loyalist, into allegations of foreign interference in the election is still ongoing.
In a private meeting Wednesday of the election committee’s members, its head, Supreme Court Justice Noam Sohlberg, read out an intelligence assessment from the Shin Bet saying the agency believed there had been a “widespread phenomenon involving the influx of substantial funds into Israel from foreign states,” including from countries hostile toward Israel.
The Shin Bet provided no evidence to explain its assertion. The Associated Press obtained a transcript of the assessment from a person who attended the meeting. The person requested anonymity to discuss a closed-door meeting.
The committee has previously said that while claims about foreign actors seeking to influence the election are serious and under investigation, it does not believe that any such interference affected the results — even if it had happened.
Sohlberg reiterated that stance on Wednesday. “At this stage, these are merely suspicions, and even if they are substantiated, the scope of their potential impact is limited,” he said during a ceremony to present the certified election results to Herzog.
He added that it was dangerous to cast doubt on the results and said they are legally binding.
Public trust in the electoral process is “easy to destroy, yet very difficult to repair,” he warned.
In the Oct. 27 vote, neither Netanyahu’s bloc nor the bloc of allies of his chief rival, opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot , secured a parliamentary majority needed to form a new government , raising the possibility of an alliance between the two rivals or an alliance between Eisenkot and some of the Arab-led parties.
Israel’s president is now expected to begin a series of sit-downs with political parties. The meetings are expected to unfold over the next several days.
Herzog is then to choose the candidate — most likely Netanyahu or Eisenkot — who he believes is most likely to be able to form a coalition government, setting the stage for weeks of negotiations.
If neither man can put together a government, the country would hold a new election early next year.
The Shin Bet had requested approval from Israel’s attorney general on Tuesday to interrogate several elected officials as part of the agency’s separate probe, including the Ra’am party leader Mansour Abbas and other senior Arab lawmakers, Israeli media reported.
The request was sharply rejected.
“It is not permissible to interrogate citizens or elected officials without evidence to justify such action,” Attorney General Gali Baharav-Miara said.
The Joint List of Arab parties condemned the request, calling it a “campaign of incitement” by Netanyahu and his allies designed to delegitimize the Arab vote.
A far-right ally of Netanyahu, Itamar Ben-Gvir, rejected the committee’s findings that the elections were valid.
He called on the Shin Bet, over which he has no jurisdiction, to “arrest all the leaders of the Arab political parties” and to interrogate them in “basement interrogation cells until these suspicions are fully clarified.”
Herzog said Wednesday that the Shin Bet investigation into possible foreign interference should play out. But he cautioned that Arab Israeli voters “must not be smeared.”
“I condemn the coarseness and racist expressions that we have heard recently,” Herzog said.
Melzer reported from Nahariya, Israel.

articles.title_orig: Trump's midterm drubbing demonstrates the power of data-centre opponents
articles.title_zh: Trump's midterm drubbing demonstrates the power of data-centre opponents
articles.content_orig:
US President Donald Trump was sharply rebuked by American voters, and he could now turn his attention to foreign policy, says Kevin Chen from the S Rajaratnam School of International Studies.
President Donald Trump gestures at a campaign rally at the Lubbock Memorial Civic Center, Tuesday, Oct. 27, 2026, in Lubbock, Texas. (AP Photo/Alex Brandon)
This audio is generated by an AI tool.
SINGAPORE: United States President Donald Trump was not on the ballot, but he had asked Americans to vote in the midterm elections as if he were.
The response was clear: Democrats have taken back control of both chambers of Congress from his Republican Party.
The election was effectively a referendum on Mr Trump’s policies: Voters were upset over his handling of the economy and related issues such as affordability. Disapproval of Mr Trump’s foreign policy, in particular the Iran War and its repercussions for energy prices, also soured voters from Republican candidates.
This frustration fuelled not just a blue wave, but a blue tsunami that Republican redistricting efforts could not block.
Democrats needed a net gain of three Republican held seats in the House of Representatives and four in the Senate to gain majorities. At the time of writing, Democrats had flipped 21 seats and seven seats in the lower and upper chambers respectively.
On paper, the Democrats will have powers to block Mr Trump’s domestic agenda and render him a “lame duck” for the remainder of his term.
With a House majority, Democrats will be able to oversee key spending bills and convene hearings to scrutinise Mr Trump’s actions. With control of the Senate, Democrats would also be able to block votes on Mr Trump’s nominees to key federal positions.
However, Mr Trump has demonstrated a willingness to bend political norms to achieve his ends. In 2019, when the Democrat-controlled Congress refused to fully fund his southern border wall, he declared a national emergency and diverted funds from other budgets to do so anyway.
Instead of a lame duck, Mr Trump might well be an “angry duck”, waging political war with his veto powers and bully pulpit.
The big unknown may well be Mr Trump’s foreign policy plans. US presidents are given significant discretion in foreign policy, allowing them to meet foreign leaders and even launch limited military strikes without Congressional approval.
Past presidents have taken advantage of this discretion. Despite the Democrat victory in the 2006 midterms, for example, then President George W Bush went ahead with the controversial 2007 surge of American troops into Iraq.
Congress’ ability to restrain a president is limited without a two-thirds majority in both chambers, and even the sweeping victories in the midterms did not deliver that. This raises deep concerns over potential escalation in the Iran War, or even Cuba.
For Asia, there are unlikely to be immediate impacts.
Facing domestic constraints and potential congressional scrutiny, Mr Trump could try to bolster his diplomatic legacy by pushing dialogue with North Korea, which would worry South Korea. But Pyongyang seems to have no appetite to entertain this.
The US could pursue its threats to slap more tariffs on trading partners, for alleged participation in what Washington calls a “transshipment scam” to route Chinese goods to evade US tariffs. Section 301 tariff investigations into several Asian economies for industrial overcapacity are also ongoing, and any legislative challenge to them will take time.
There is also uncertainty over the election’s implications for US-China relations. Mr Trump’s two upcoming meetings with Chinese President Xi Jinping will take place before the House reopens in January 2027, making any legislative disruption unlikely.
In any case, before the Democrat-controlled Congress tries to insert itself into the relationship of “constructive strategic stability”, they would need to settle internal debates over their stance on China policy.
Yet, the divided government in Washington should not be seen as a reason for regional governments to dial back engagement. US national security interests, particularly over rare earths and supply chains, are not going to change overnight.
It is still more prudent to work with the US where interests align and build trust than to hold back and wait for a new occupant in the White House.
Kevin Chen is an Associate Research Fellow with the US Programme at the S Rajaratnam School of International Studies (RSIS), Nanyang Technological University (NTU), Singapore.

articles.title_orig: Private companies added 86,000 jobs in October, slightly higher than expected, ADP says
articles.title_zh: Private companies added 86,000 jobs in October, slightly higher than expected, ADP says
articles.content_orig:
Private sector job growth held steady in October, with gains spread across sectors, as the labor market showed fresh signs of stabilization, ADP reported Wednesday.
The payrolls processing firm said companies added 86,000 jobs during the month, the same as the downwardly revised total for September and slightly ahead of the Dow Jones estimate for 75,000.
Employment gains came mainly in the service sector.
Trade, transportation and utilities led with 39,000 new jobs, while education and health services added 28,000, and leisure and hospitality contributed 19,000. Other sectors showing gains included financial activities (15,000), construction (13,000) and other services (10,000).
However, some of the gains were offset by a decline of 27,000 in professional and business services and a loss of 8,000 in natural resources and mining. Information services, a sector potentially impacted by the artificial intelligence buildout, lost 2,000 jobs.
Salaries continued to show gains, particularly for those changing jobs — those workers saw a 4.8% annual gain. A report Tuesday from the Bureau of Labor Statistics showed that the number of people quitting their job, a sign of labor market mobility, hit its highest level since March 2025.
Workers overall saw a 3.2% base pay gain, while gross pay increased 4.7% annually. Pay for those staying in their jobs rose 3%.
"Employers of all sizes were hiring last month, and our data suggests that job-changers were lured by a combination of bonuses, overtime, and more hours in addition to higher base pay," said ADP's chief economist, Nela Richardson. "Taken together, earnings growth for these workers hit its fastest pace since March 2024."
Companies with between 50 and 499 workers added 33,000 jobs. Large businesses added 24,000, while small firms increased rolls by 28,000.
The ADP report serves as a precursor to the BLS nonfarm payrolls count to be released Friday.
Economists surveyed by Dow Jones are looking for the BLS report for October to show a gain of 59,000 after September's modest growth of 29,000.

articles.title_orig: U.S. Marine dies in Japan during training, military says
articles.title_zh: U.S. Marine dies in Japan during training, military says
articles.content_orig:
A United States Marine has died in Japan, following a “training incident,” the military said in a statement Wednesday.
The unnamed Marine was undertaking training at Camp Schwab in Okinawa, Japan’s southernmost prefecture, the statement said. The area is home to a large U.S. military presence and bases that serve as a regional hub in the Indo-Pacific.
The Marine who was with the 3rd Marine Division died Tuesday and will not be named until 24 hours after the individual’s family has been notified, the 3rd Marine Division said in a statement Wednesday.
“It is with heavy hearts that 3rd Marine Division announces the death of a Marine following a training incident at Camp Schwab, Okinawa, Japan, on Nov. 3, 2026,” the statement said.
“The circumstances surrounding the incident remain under investigation,” it added. “We express our deepest condolences to the family and loved ones of our Marine.”
Okinawa was under U.S. occupation following World War II until it was handed back to Japan in 1972. Today, the U.S. population on the island is nearly 80,000, with nearly 30,000 being active duty troops from all four branches of the armed forces, though the Marines make up the bulk of the forces.
Separately, Secretary of State Marco Rubio last month pledged to cooperate with Japanese authorities investigating allegations that a ​U.S. Marine murdered a woman in Okinawa. The case sparked widespread protests and led to a U.S. military curfew and mandatory training in standards and discipline.
Lt. Gen. Benjamin Watson, commander of the III Marine Expeditionary Force, said at the time that serving on the Japanese island “comes with responsibility.”
Adela Suliman is a breaking-news editor and reporter for NBC News in London.
