articles.title_orig: Apple's first touchscreen MacBook comes at a price
articles.title_zh: Apple's first touchscreen MacBook comes at a price
articles.content_orig:
People try out the new MacBook Pro with a touchscreen following the launch by Apple CEO John Ternus in Los Angeles, on Oct. 28, 2026. (REUTERS)
Apple has finally given the MacBook Pro something many people have wanted for years: a touchscreen. The company unveiled its first touchscreen MacBook Pro on Oct. 28, introducing a new way to interact with its laptop. It also brings a stunning OLED display, a thinner design and some serious processing power. However, there's one detail that might make you think twice before reaching for your wallet. The new touchscreen MacBook Pro starts at $2,899.
That's a lot of money for a laptop, even by Apple's standards. So, what exactly are you getting for that price? More importantly, will touching your MacBook's screen make enough of a difference to justify an upgrade? Let's look at what Apple has introduced and who might benefit most.
Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover 5 ways to travel smarter and save money.
Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways to protect your phone and personal information, avoid common travel scams, find better deals, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed.
Watch the free replay + downloadable checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com.
8 BIGGEST THINGS WE LEARNED FROM APPLE'S 2026 EVENT
Apple's first touchscreen MacBook Pro lets users interact directly with the display, bringing familiar iPhone and iPad gestures to the Mac. (Apple)
For years, Apple maintained that the Mac worked best with a keyboard and trackpad. Meanwhile, Windows laptop owners have enjoyed touchscreen options for a long time. Apple even experimented with touch controls through its Touch Bar, but that feature never replaced the traditional laptop experience.
Now Apple has changed course. Its new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display lets you interact directly with the screen. You can scroll through websites with your finger or pinch to zoom into photos. Apple also lets you drag content between windows and interact with supported creative apps.
Think about how often you instinctively touch your laptop screen, especially after spending years using an iPhone or iPad. Now that gesture will actually do something on the new MacBook Pro. Apple also redesigned the hinge to keep the display steadier when you touch it. That's a thoughtful addition because nobody wants a screen wobbling every time they tap a button.
However, this remains a traditional laptop. It doesn't fold into a tablet, and it doesn't support Apple Pencil. You'll still use the keyboard and trackpad for much of your work. That may disappoint anyone hoping to replace both a MacBook and an iPad with one device.
While everyone is talking about the touchscreen, Apple's new display technology might have an even greater impact on your everyday experience. The company calls it the PROLED XDR Display, and it uses tandem OLED technology. Unlike traditional laptop screens that rely on a backlight, OLED pixels produce their own light. That allows the display to show deep blacks alongside bright highlights without the same backlight glow.
Apple says the new screen reaches up to 2,000 nits of peak brightness for both HDR and SDR content. It also delivers a claimed 10,000,000:1 contrast ratio and supports refresh rates up to 120Hz for smoother motion. Those numbers sound impressive, but what will you actually notice?
Apple CEO John Ternus mingles at the launch of a new MacBook Pro with a touch screen in Los Angeles on Oct. 28, 2026. (REUTERS)
Photos should look more vibrant, especially when you're viewing pictures taken on your iPhone. Movies can show more detail in dark scenes. If you edit videos or work with photography, the improved color accuracy could be especially useful.
Apple has also added an antireflective coating to help reduce glare. An optional nano-texture finish provides additional reflection control for people who work in bright environments. For someone who spends hours looking at a laptop screen, these improvements could be more valuable than touch alone.
Apple isn't holding back on performance. The new touchscreen MacBook Pro comes with either an M5 Pro or M5 Max processor . Both target people who need more processing power than a basic laptop typically provides. If you're editing high-resolution video or working with large photo libraries, these chips are designed to handle that workload. Apple also offers configurations with up to 128GB of unified memory and 16TB of storage. However, those upgrades can drive the price considerably higher.
The new MacBook Pro runs macOS 27 and includes Apple Intelligence alongside Apple's upgraded Siri AI. It also brings Dynamic Island to the Mac for the first time. That familiar feature from the iPhone sits near the top of the display and gives you access to live updates and useful controls. For video calls, Apple includes a 12-megapixel Center Stage camera. Meanwhile, an upgraded six-speaker system promises deeper bass. The laptop also includes Thunderbolt 5 connectivity and an HDMI port, which should appeal to people connecting external displays.
12 BIGGEST APPLE WWDC 2026 TAKEAWAYS YOU NEED TO KNOW
Apple's new touchscreen MacBook Pro comes in 14-inch and 16-inch models, with prices starting at $2,899. (Apple)
One concern with touchscreen laptops is whether all that additional technology makes them heavier. Apple says it has managed to move in the opposite direction. The new 14-inch touchscreen MacBook Pro weighs about three pounds, roughly half a pound less than its predecessor. The 16-inch model comes in at four pounds, approximately 0.7 pounds lighter. Both models also feature slimmer designs. That should make carrying a MacBook Pro between meetings or packing one for a trip a little easier.
Apple promises up to 24 hours of battery life, depending on the configuration and usage. That's an impressive claim for a machine with this much performance and such a bright display. However, we'll need independent testing to see how battery life holds up during real-world work.
Apple has positioned its touchscreen MacBook Pro firmly in premium territory. The 14-inch model with the M5 Pro chip starts at $2,899, while the 16-inch version starts at $3,399. If you want the more powerful M5 Max processor, prices jump to $4,499 for the 14-inch model and $4,799 for the 16-inch version. And remember, those are starting prices for each configuration. Adding more memory or storage can increase the total substantially.
There is another important detail. Apple introduced a separate 14-inch MacBook Pro with its newer M6 chip on Oct. 27. That model starts at $1,999, but it uses a Liquid Retina XDR Display without touch support. That means you're looking at a $900 difference between Apple's entry-level M6 MacBook Pro and its least expensive touchscreen model. Of course, the more expensive version also includes an M5 Pro processor and the upgraded OLED display. These are different performance configurations, so the additional $900 doesn't represent the cost of touch alone.
For another perspective, the previous 14-inch MacBook Pro with the M5 Pro chip started at $2,499. That makes the new touchscreen version $400 more expensive than its comparable predecessor. Still, this gives you a meaningful choice. You can buy a powerful new MacBook Pro for considerably less if you don't need to interact directly with the screen. We've previously reported on how rising AI chip costs have pushed Apple prices higher. This latest introduction adds another premium option to an already expensive lineup.
Apple says many existing Mac apps will respond to touch immediately because macOS can translate finger taps into mouse clicks. That should make basic interaction straightforward, even before developers fully optimize their software.

articles.title_orig: Apple still charging 300% of costs on iPhone storage upgrades, says WSJ
articles.title_zh: Apple still charging 300% of costs on iPhone storage upgrades, says WSJ
articles.content_orig:
Opting for more RAM or storage when buying Apple devices has always been an expensive business, with the company famously charging huge markups.
Apple said in its most recent earnings report that even after the price increases, its margins are being squeezed by higher component costs. But an analysis suggests that the company is still charging three times its own costs for higher storage tiers on the iPhone 18 Pro …
To be fair to Apple, some of the criticism about the premiums charged on configuring a device with more memory or flash storage hasn’t been comparing, well, apples with apples. The SSDs used in Macs, for example, are very much faster than the lower-spec third-party storage cards people typically cite as evidence for the company’s greed.
All the same, there’s no denying that the iPhone maker has always applied extremely high markups to its own direct costs. With the iPhone 17 Pro, for example, upgrading from 256GB to 1TB cost a buyer $400. A Wall Street Journal analysis cited by Macworld says that Apple’s cost at the time was $42, almost a 1,000% markup.
Apple this week warned that memory costs will reduce its holiday quarter profit margins .
When you remove the tariff refunds from both the June and September quarters, both company and product gross margin would be down about one point sequentially, primarily driven by higher memory costs. Parekh added that the pressure on Apple’s margins isn’t expected to ease anytime soon.
However, the WSJ’s number-crunching suggests that we probably don’t need to get out the violins just yet. The paper compared the same upgrade on the iPhone 18 Pro, where Apple has increased the price difference to $600. Although the Cupertino company is paying dramatically more, with an estimated direct cost of $192, that still amounts to customers being charged more than three times the price paid by Apple.

The integration of Call of Duty: Warzone with Modern Warfare 4 is happening on November 6 when Season 1 begins for this year's game.
While it also means the end of Warzone for players on Xbox One and PS4 , it will be bringing a bunch of new content to the table. When the switchover happens, there will be two brand-new maps to play at first, alongside two returning classic maps at some point later in the season.
Besides access to all the new weapons from Modern Warfare 4, the battle pass, the leveling and prestige system, Camo challenges, and Calling Cards, there are also some quality-of-life improvements, too. Here's a brief overview of what's coming.
At the launch of Season 1 there will be two Warzone maps to play, and they're both brand-new for the Modern Warfare 4 year: Hajin and Zodiac.
Zodiac we've already seen during the Modern Warfare 4 beta period earlier this year. Set around a drone manufacturing facility in South Korea, Zodiac is the new Resurgence map and will be joined in the rotation by the returning Rebirth Island at some point during the season.
Hajin is the new "big map" for Battle Royale. Set across North and South Korea, anyone who's already jumped in to play DMZ will be familiar with the Hajin location. It appears to be the same physical map, so those players will already have a leg up on the terrain.
It's been a pretty good location for DMZ so far, and while there are areas with tall buildings, there are also plenty that are more open, and the terrain is quite varied. Also coming across from DMZ is the variable weather, so one match it might be sunny and clear, and another the map may be shrouded in fog. Hajin will also have two new Gulags.
The previous big map, Verdansk, will be joining the Battle Royale rotation at some point during the season, bringing some new POIs along with it.
Besides the new map, there are also some new features and just overall quality-of-life improvements for Warzone beginning with Season 1. These include:
Tactical Sprint is probably a big one for Warzone players, and while it doesn't sound like it will be overpowered, it will at least help in keeping that fast-flowing experience players have become familiar with.
Without it applied in multiplayer in Modern Warfare 4, you can feel quite slow, and that was never going to work in Warzone.
It'll be interesting to see what the weapon balancing looks like, though. Additionally, the time to kill (TTK). In DMZ, PvP encounters are often over before you even spot who's firing at you, so hopefully Warzone has found a balance here. There are definitely some weapons that already feel like everyone will gravitate towards them, but it'd be nice if there's a wider meta than there often is.
All of the weapons from Modern Warfare 4 and the new ones introduced in Season 1 will be available to Warzone players, as will their attachments, including Apex.
Legacy weapons from as far back as Modern Warfare 2 will remain accessible in Warzone. These will be available as a five-attachment version, alongside any previously acquired legacy weapon blueprints.
Additionally, and what sounds quite interesting to me, is that on Hajin, Zodiac, and Verdansk, we'll now have movable interactive objects. These include fuel barrels, which will go boom, and apparently objects such as dumpsters and "pyramids" that can be used to create cover. Or roadblocks. So maybe keep an extra eye out when you're driving.
Players will also be able to get their hands on Elite Perks, which will add a fourth perk to their loadout. These are found in-match at Buy Stations, and more can be obtained through Supply Run contracts. But only one can be active at a time.
Oh, and the Aston Martin Dreadnought vehicle that we've been driving about in DMZ will also be joining Warzone.
Camo grinders will be delighted to hear that casual mode has returned for both Battle Royale and Resurgence and will be available on all maps.
Additionally, at Season 1 launch there will be three limited-time modes (LTMs):
Additional LTMs are promised throughout Season 1, including Rockets and Snipers, and Extreme Resurgence.
Rally Point is described as a casual mode designed to help new and returning players get to grips with the mechanics of Warzone, as well as check out the new Zodiac map and learn about some of the new features. 20 players will be in each lobby.
"Rally Point is a no-circle, infinite Resurgence, and Drop-In/Drop-Out mode, allowing players to come and go as they please."
For completing the challenges in this mode, there will be an exclusive weapon blueprint and two camos to unlock.
Loaded Resurgence will be across Zodiac and Rebirth Island and looks the same as we've known it before. Drop in with your preferred loadout and earn new perks with eliminations as you try to get to Specialist.
Massive Resurgence is Resurgence, but on the Hajin big map with 120 players. There aren't any special rewards listed for these modes right now, but that doesn't mean there won't be some.
While much of the camo grind in Modern Warfare 4 is universal across multiplayer, DMZ, and now Warzone, like the others, there is a dedicated set of Mode Mastery challenges to complete. And now we know what we'll have to do.
Presumably we'll still be able to do the Mode Mastery camos in casual mode, too, but even so, they're still going to be a pretty long process. The saving grace is that if you've been playing Modern Warfare 4, this year you at least already have a head start.
Nevertheless, I spent 65 hours doing last year's Warzone Mastery Camo, even using casual mode, and I feel like this year's is going to take longer than that. I'm not sure I have it in me. We'll see.
Additionally, there will be a "Return to Call of Duty: Warzone" event running with some additional camos to get your hands on. And who doesn't like some shiny camos?
Season 1 for both Modern Warfare 4 and Warzone goes live on November 6 at midnight ET (9pm Pacific) globally. Additionally, it will be available on the Nintendo Switch for the first time. Find the full details on the Warzone integration at the Call of Duty Blog .

Founder Summit begins Nov. 4, 9:00 a.m. ET. Get your pass savings & deals before it starts. REGISTER HERE.
Design software maker Canva is cutting 22% of its staff, amounting to 1,271 people, amid a growth slowdown.
The company’s co-founder and CEO, Melanie Perkins, in a note to employees said while Canva has scaled so far, it needs to change to address slowing growth.
“Over the past thirteen years, we’ve turned a dream in a pitch deck into a platform used by hundreds of millions of people. None of it would have been possible without the talent, imagination, and care of every single person who has been part of this journey. Yet success in our first chapter doesn’t guarantee success in the next. This has been our hardest year yet, and as we shared earlier this year, our growth has slowed for the first time in a decade,” Perkins wrote.
Canva is reshuffling its organizational chart and merging its product, growth and platform teams to reduce communication friction. The company is also reducing “subspecialisation,” which means its employees might be asked to take up more responsibilities. The company is also moving towards hybrid work and asking people to work from an office a few days a week.
The company has been shipping its own AI models to reduce costs and reliance on third-party models, but it still had to cut its revenue growth forecast to 20% from 30% to address ballooning AI costs. This also resulted in Canva’s early investors cutting its valuation to about $35 billion earlier this year.
Canva is also facing increasing competition from AI startups and general-purpose chatbots like ChatGPT and Gemini, whose image generation capabilities allow people to easily put together posters and presentations.

articles.title_orig: Anthropic is an opportunity to rethink IPO rules
articles.title_zh: Anthropic is an opportunity to rethink IPO rules
articles.content_orig:
Anthropic reported updated financials as part of an amended Form S-1 filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission on Monday, giving investors a more comprehensive look into the state of its business.
The artificial intelligence company said it generated $33.24 billion in revenue for the nine months ended Sept. 30, up roughly 1,200% from the same period last year. It reported a $104 billion net loss during the period, though most of that was due to the change in fair value of convertible notes and derivative liabilities. Anthropic had a loss of $25.1 billion over the same stretch in 2025.
Anthropic unveiled its highly anticipated prospectus last week, bringing the company one step closer to a potentially historic initial public offering . The initial filing only included the Claude maker's financials through the first half of the year.
During its third quarter, Anthropic generated roughly $17 billion in revenue, up about 1,127% from the same period last year. Revenue growth slowed on a quarter-to-quarter basis, however. Third-quarter revenue increased around 47%, a steep drop from 144% growth in Q2 and 132% in Q1.
The company reported a net loss of $23.29 billion during its third quarter.
As the 5-year-old company prepares to kick off its roadshow, it will have to reckon with growing market jitters around the AI buildout. Wall Street has been worried that rising interest rates will make debt unaffordable for many data center developers and neoclouds , and quarterly reports from Microsoft , Alphabet and Amazon last week added fuel to those concerns.
The hyperscalers' aggressive AI spending is eating into their cash flows , causing some investors to worry that computing capacity may not come online quickly enough to meet Anthropic's demands. Anthropic gets much of its capacity from Amazon, Google and SpaceX , but it also relies on neoclouds for some compute as it races to expand as quickly as possible.
In the amended S-1, Anthropic said it has entered into purchase commitments and lease agreements with an aggregate committed spend of about $895.4 billion, "substantially all of which is related to compute and infrastructure."
Anthropic said its compute and infrastructure expenses increased by $14.4 billion for the nine months ended Sept. 30, up 329% compared with the same period last year.
"As our compute and infrastructure capacity grows, the associated compute and infrastructure expenses have increased," Anthropic said in the filing.
The company's CEO, Dario Amodei, co-founded Anthropic alongside a handful of other researchers who defected from OpenAI , now its chief rival. OpenAI confidentially filed its prospectus with the SEC in June, but its executives have signaled that it's aiming for a 2027 debut .
Anthropic has worked to position itself as more safety-conscious than its competitors, and its S-1 includes more than 90 pages of risk factors . The company highlights risks, including potential political headwinds, its complex infrastructure needs as well as the difficulties that can come from balancing safety and commercial objectives.
"We consider it our personal responsibility to help the world understand these risks, to prevent or mitigate them when they arise from our AI models, and to work with governments and the rest of the industry to address them at a societal level," Anthropic's co-founders said in the filing.

articles.title_orig: CVS falls 14% on plans to split off drugstore business in major breakup of healthcare giant
articles.title_zh: CVS falls 14% on plans to split off drugstore business in major breakup of healthcare giant
articles.content_orig:
CVS Health plans to split into two separate public companies by the first half 2028 in what would be one of the largest corporate splits in history, the company announced Wednesday.
The move would reverse the company's massive $78 billion acquisition of its insurer, Aetna, and dismantle the vertically integrated healthcare conglomerate it created in 2018. The plan would specifically separate CVS' roughly 9,000 retail pharmacies from its major insurance business and pharmacy benefit manager, Caremark, one of the nation's three largest PBMs.
The decision follows a "comprehensive strategic review" by the company's board of directors, according to a news release . Shares of CVS fell roughly 11% on Wednesday.
It's a stunning reversal for the healthcare powerhouse, which has spent the last two decades working to turn itself into a one-stop health destination. The move also comes as CVS' aggressive turnaround plan under CEO David Joyner shows substantial progress, with the company pursuing $2 billion in cost cuts, store closures, leadership shakeups and efforts to rein in Medicare Advantage costs.
But Joyner told CNBC's "Squawk on the Street" on Wednesday that the decision to split is "out of a position of strength," pointing to recovery in Aetna's Medicare business and solid performance in the retail pharmacy.
"So it's all about the strength of the business that affords us the opportunity to make what we think are the right strategic decisions for the future of this company," he later added.
CVS shares have jumped roughly 70% since Joyner took the helm in October 2024, bringing the company's market value to $117 billion.
The two new companies would both be publicly traded.
The insurance and PBM company will retain the CVS Health name and be run by Joyner, while the other company will be called CVS Pharmacy and be led by Prem Shah, who is currently group president of CVS Health. Additional leadership positions and board members will be announced at a later date, CVS said.
Existing CVS shareholders will own shares in both companies after the split. The Financial Times on Tuesday first reported the breakup plans.
The company's pharmacy business raked in $37.66 billion in 2025 sales, while its insurance unit booked $36.29 billion in revenue and healthcare services segment generated $51.24 billion.
CVS on Wednesday also posted third-quarter earnings and revenue that topped Wall Street expectations. Total sales climbed to $108.40 billion, from $102.87 billion in the prior-year period.
Sales were boosted by year-over-year growth in the company's health care benefits and health services segments. Meanwhile, revenue in its pharmacy services business slid from the previous year.
On Wednesday, CVS said it will lump its insurer and PBM with its primary care business Oak Street Health, home-visit provider Signify Health and the company's specialty drug business.
CVS also said the split will allow the two companies to experience a "focused strategic agenda" and greater ability to "innovate, adopt technology, increase efficiency," among other benefits.
It's not the first time CVS has weighed splitting the company. In October 2024, CVS engaged advisors in a strategic review of its business and considered breaking up its retail pharmacy and insurance units.
But Joyner told CNBC that the company was "in a turnaround" at that time without the flexibility, cash position or business performance to execute a split.
In an interview, Leerink Partners analyst Michael Cherny said the split shows "the stability of the pharmacy," which has won market share from competitors and is seeing gross margins stabilize thanks to CostVantage, a new pharmacy reimbursement model introduced by CVS last year that the company bills as more transparent.
"This business is a much different business from the one that's been considered three years ago, five years ago, 10 years ago, where there had been a litany of headwinds that the pharmacy just couldn't overcome," he told CNBC on Wednesday.
One potential concern for investors is whether the retail pharmacy will lose its competitive advantage of being directly linked with a PBM, which negotiates drug prices and manages prescription drug benefits on behalf of insurers and employers.
But Joyner told analysts Wednesday that the synergy between the two businesses "are going to be preserved in commercial agreements between the two organizations," adding that "we don't need the integration of an operating structure."
Cherny said the rationale for the split could also extend to the state legislative scrutiny over the company's level of vertical integration.
The potential breakup also comes as pharmacy benefit managers face mounting bipartisan scrutiny in Washington, D.C., and across states. Republicans in Tennessee and Arkansas have passed laws that would ban co-ownership of PBMs and pharmacies. Those have been challenged in court by CVS and other companies.
PBMs have been criticized for opaque pricing practices, their growing market power and potential conflicts of interest when they are owned by companies that also operate insurers and pharmacies.

articles.title_orig: AI data center stocks dip, renewables surge after Democrat sweep in US midterm elections
articles.title_zh: AI data center stocks dip, renewables surge after Democrat sweep in US midterm elections
articles.content_orig:
Democrats scored sweeping victories in the U.S. midterm elections on Wednesday, flipping key Republican-held seats in Congress and securing historic wins in traditionally conservative states, as voters delivered a setback to President Donald Trump.
The party was projected to gain control of both chambers of Congress, with victories across several battleground states threatening to constrain Trump's legislative agenda for the remaining two years of his presidency.
Here are some of the scenes from polling stations, campaign headquarters and election-night celebrations across the United States.
Among the biggest surprises was Texas, where Democrat James Talarico defeated Republican Ken Paxton to become the state's first Democratic U.S. senator since 1988.
Fellow Democrat Gina Hinojosa also unseated Republican Gov. Greg Abbott, becoming the state's first Latina governor and ending more than three decades of Republican control of the office.
In North Carolina, former Democratic Gov. Roy Cooper flipped a Republican-held Senate seat after defeating Trump-backed Michael Whatley. Cooper will succeed retiring Republican Sen. Thom Tillis, who announced his departure after clashing with Trump over his tax and spending legislation.
In Georgia, Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff secured reelection against Trump-backed Republican Mike Collins, while former Atlanta Mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms won the governor's race, becoming the first Black woman elected governor of a U.S. state.
Meanwhile, in Ohio, former Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown staged a political comeback, defeating Republican incumbent Jon Husted in a closely watched Senate race.
The elections were widely viewed as a referendum on Trump's second term, with concerns over the cost of living, inflation and the war in Iran weighing on voter sentiment.
—CNBC's Danielle DeVries contributed to this article.

articles.title_orig: Dow futures rally 700 points as Democrats win big in midterms: Live updates
articles.title_zh: Dow futures rally 700 points as Democrats win big in midterms: Live updates
articles.content_orig:
Stock futures ripped higher on Wednesday, reversing earlier losses, as a decisive victory by Democrats in the U.S. midterm elections allowed investors to look past the political risk hanging over the market.
Futures tied to the Dow Jones Industrial Average jumped 724 points, or 1.4%. S&P 500 futures traded 1% higher, along with Nasdaq-100 futures . Stock futures were down sharply overnight.
Democrats took control of Congress Tuesday night, winning majorities in both the House and Senate. They also scored victories in key gubernatorial races, including Texas.
Heading into the election investors worried a Democratic sweep could weigh on some areas of the market , especially stocks related to the artificial intelligence build-out. Wall Street also worried that a clear winner would not emerge Tuesday night. However, those concerns eased after President Donald Trump said he was willing to accept the election results and work with Democrats.
Elon Musk's SpaceX was down 4.8% in premarket trading, while Tesla shares shed 4.9%. Neocloud stocks CoreWeave and Nebius fell 3.6% and 1%, respectively.
But other parts of the tech trade gained. Microsoft advanced 0.3%, and Amazon climbed 1.1%, as Nvidia moved 0.5% higher. Alphabet was the outlier, trading around 0.4% lower.
U.S. health insurers and hospital operators also advanced, with United Health up 1.4%, Molina Healthcare rising 6.3%, Centene adding 4.7% and HCA Healthcare up 1.44%.
Renewables stocks rallied sharply in premarket trading, while defense stocks fell.
AMD shares popped 6% after the chipmaker reported third-quarter earnings and revenue that blew past analyst expectations.
Andrew Slimmon of Morgan Stanley Investment Management said the result will bring "gridlock" to Washington, but added that the markets "like gridlock — they don't like a party with too much power."
Speaking with CNBC's "Squawk Box Europe", Slimmon said that if the result increases the push for a resolution to the Middle East conflict, that may bring oil prices lower.  "That's been an issue for the Fed, and inflation, and part of the reason that rates are higher."
Renewable shares like solar stocks traded higher in the post-market on speculation a Democratic majority in Congress would halt policies by President Donald Trump taken against the industry. The Invesco Solar ETF was up 3% in Robinhood trading.
President Donald Trump may have helped ease pressure on the market a bit overnight by not challenging the midterm results in an interview with the Wall Street Journal . Trump told the WSJ, "I think we'll work with the Democrats, and we'll get along very well with them."
Nasdaq-100 futures are up 929.75 points off their overnight lows, based on the current price of 28,545.50. Futures contracts tied to the benchmark hit a low of 27,615.75,  their lowest since July 30.
Precious metals saw strong gains on Wednesday morning as the Democrats scored a clean sweep in the midterm elections, flipping both the House and Senate.
Spot gold was 2.93% higher at $4,043.45 an ounce by 5:05 a.m. ET, while spot silver jumped 4.44% to trade at $51.98 per ounce, as traders reacted to the U.S. midterm election results.
Front-month gold futures added 2.9% to trade at $4,054.60, while silver futures were up 4.64% at $52.09.
Other metals seeing notable gains on Wednesday morning included platinum , which jumped 2.47% to trade at $1,465.30, and palladium, which was 5.93% higher at $989.
Renewables and healthcare shares are among the biggest premarket movers, trading higher after Democrats took control of the House and Senate. Meanwhile, neocloud stocks, as well as prison operators and defense names, lag the broader market.
U.S. renewable energy stocks climbed on expectations of a policy shift. First Solar advanced 8.5%, Bloom Energy gained 5.8%, Plug Power rose 10.6%, Sunrun notched an 8.64% gain, FuelCell Energy was up 6.24% and SolarEdge Technologies moved 4% higher.
Healthcare stocks also rose. UnitedHealth gained 1.8%, Molina Healthcare added 6.3%, Centene climbed 5% and HCA Healthcare advanced 7.16%.
Neocloud stocks, in contrast, turned lower, with CoreWeave down 3.6% and Nebius off 1%. Shares of prison operators and defense names also fell.
European renewable energy stocks moved sharply higher in early trade as prospects of a decisive Democrat victory in the U.S. midterm elections sparked hopes of a U.S. policy shift on renewables.
Copenhagen-listed Oersted surged 7.3% while Danish peer Vestas advanced 5.2%. The two companies have grappled with uncertainty in their U.S. businesses in recent years, partly as a result of fierce opposition from the Trump administration toward the renewable energy sector.
SMA Solar shares were up 5.5% and Nordex shares added 4.8%.
The pan-European Stoxx 600 added 0.44% in early trading, as the continent's stocks and major bourses moved higher on the Democrats' clean sweep of the U.S. midterms.
Banks advanced 1.83%, leading gains, with basic resources up 1.71% and utilities rising 0.68%. Food and beverage stocks lost 0.57%, and industrial goods fell 0.37%.
The Italian FTSE MIB was up 0.88%, leading regional bourses. The U.K.'s FTSE 100 added 0.22%, while the French CAC 40 rose 0.24% and Germany's DAX gained 0.28%.
Novo posted quarterly earnings ahead of expectations early Wednesday as sales of its Wegovy pill blew past estimates amid continued GLP-1 volume growth globally, sending shares up as much as 6% in early trading.
The company updated its outlook to now see adjusted revenue and operating profit growth between negative 2% and 2% at constant exchange rates. It previously saw full-year sales and operating profits, which it hiked in August, at negative 6% to flat for both metrics.
Sales in the third quarter came in at 79.2 billion Danish kroner ($11.9 billion), up 4% year-on-year at constant exchange rates and ahead of FactSet estimates of 73.6 billion kroner. Adjusted operating profit (EBIT) was 31.7 billion kroner, compared with the expected 28.6 billion kroner.
It comes as the Danish weight-loss drug maker is looking to regain momentum following a tumultuous year in which it fell behind rival Eli Lilly.
Asia-Pacific markets closed mixed Wednesday, as investors assessed a projected Democratic takeover of the U.S. Senate and House, while President Donald Trump appeared to not challenge the results.
"We'll work with the Democrats, and we'll get along very well with them," Trump told the Wall Street Journal.
South Korea's Kospi rose 0.62% to end at 5,683.8, while the small-cap, tech-focused Kosdaq added 1.5% to 714.95 in choppy trading.
Japan's Nikkei 225 pared some losses to close 1.42% lower at 62,188.63, and the broad-based Topix declined 0.89% to 3,895.38.
Mainland China's CSI 300 gained 2.31% to 4,101.34, while Hong Kong's Hang Seng Index was 1.43% higher in its last hour of trade.
Australia's S&P/ASX 200 fell 0.59% to 8,834.5.
— Lee Ying Shan, Lim Hui Jie
The dollar moved lower against most major currencies as the Democrats took control of Congress after the U.S. midterm elections.
The euro was last seen 0.39% higher against the dollar at $1.1235, while the British pound also strengthened against the greenback, rising 0.48% to $1.3476.
The dollar index , which tracks the greenback's strength against a basket of six major currencies, was down 0.39% at $101.32.
Treasury yields moved lower on Wednesday as investors sought shelter from a sell-off in equity futures sparked by potential big victories from Democrats in the U.S. midterm elections.
The benchmark 10-year Treasury note yield was last seen 1 basis point lower at 4.9311%. The 30-year bond yield slipped 1 basis point to 5.3136%, and the shorter-term 2-year note yield pulled back 1 basis point to 4.6017%.
European stock markets are set to open negative as investors respond to overnight projections of a major Democratic victory in the U.S. midterms.
The Democrats are projected to win both chambers of Congress, according to The Associated Press.

articles.title_zh: China calls for constructive ties with US amid Democratic gains in midterm elections
articles.content_orig:
The Democratic Party has regained control of the lower chamber of the United States Congress, winning the House of Representatives.
Late on Tuesday night local time, the House result was called in favour of the left-wing party.
Democrats needed to gain five seats to flip the chamber. Republicans have held a majority in the House since the 2022 midterms, during the presidency of Democrat Joe Biden.
The outgoing 119th House has 218 Republicans, 214 Democrats, one independent and two vacancies.
All 435 seats in the House were up for grabs in the election. A term in the House lasts only two years, compared with six for the Senate.
The Democrats’ victory in the House means their party leader in the chamber, Representative Hakeem Jeffries of New York, will likely be selected as the speaker, the chamber’s top officer.
That position would make Jeffries the third in line for the US presidency, should the president and the vice president be removed from office.
He would also be the first Black person to serve in the role. He will replace outgoing Republican Speaker Mike Johnson of Louisiana, who has held the post since 2023.
Democrats had been widely projected to regain control of the House, leveraging backlash to the second administration of President Donald Trump, which saw record-low approval ratings in the weeks leading up to the midterms.
For the last two years, Trump’s Republican Party has held a political “trifecta” in Washington, DC, with control of the presidency and both chambers of Congress. The 120th Congress is slated to be sworn in on January 3, 2027.
Democrats swept Republican-held House seats on their way to retaking the chamber.
In Iowa, Democrat Sarah Trone Garriott unseated Republican Zach Nunn in the state’s 3rd Congressional District.
In Virginia, Democrat Elaine Luria won a tight race against Republican incumbent Jen Kiggans, while in Pennsylvania’s 10th Congressional District, Democrat Janelle Stelson unseated seven-term Republican Scott Perry.
Meanwhile, Democrat incumbents Ilhan Omar and Ro Khanna sailed to victory, holding on to their seats in Minnesota and California.
Reacting to the Democratic wave, former President Barack Obama said the results showed voters wanted leaders who would bring people together and offer solutions to the problems they face.
“Tonight, the American people sent a clear message,” Obama wrote on X. He praised candidates who ran in areas long considered difficult for Democrats to win and urged supporters to keep organising during Trump’s remaining two years in office.
Senator Bernie Sanders said Democratic control of both chambers would allow the party to “hold Trump accountable”.
He urged Democrats to tackle income and wealth inequality. “We must aggressively fight for working families. No more excuses,” Sanders said.
Even Trump issued rare praise for the Democratic campaign in an interview with Fox News.
“I think the Democrats did a good job. I really do. I think they did a good job. They fought hard,” the president said.

articles.title_orig: Stocks, dollar slide as stunning victories for Democrats jolt AI bets
articles.title_zh: Stocks, dollar slide as stunning victories for Democrats jolt AI bets
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
SINGAPORE, Nov 4 (Reuters) - Global stocks slumped and the dollar hit a one-month low on Wednesday as Democrats gained control of both the Senate and the House in the US midterm elections, fuelling fears that rapid AI sector growth could be hamstrung by regulatory scrutiny.
In ‌a major setback to President Donald Trump, Democrats notched up victories in the South Carolina, Texas and Ohio Senate races, capturing majorities in both the ‌Senate and House that reached deep into Republican strongholds.
The breadth of the party's success was underscored by gains in districts long considered safely conservative, highlighting a political shift that caught many investors off guard.
AI stocks ​were quick to slide. That in turn put the dollar under pressure, while cryptocurrencies also fell at the prospect of stronger regulations. Bonds, though, found favour as investors sought safer assets.
"Tighter regulatory scrutiny of technology and AI companies along with the higher likelihood of political gridlock beckon with a Democrat sweep," said Prashant Newnaha, senior rates strategist at TD Securities in Singapore.
The AI boom has helped propel global markets in recent years, driven by heavy spending from tech giants racing to build data centres and expand computing capacity. That has ‌left investors acutely sensitive to anything that could derail the ⁠technology's rapid expansion.
The election outcome could also hold broad implications for the US fiscal outlook as well as sectors such as defence, healthcare and banking.
S&P 500 futures were last down 0.35% while Nasdaq futures skidded more than 2% before cutting losses to trade down 0.5%. ⁠European futures were down 0.4%, having slid 1.5% earlier.
"Looks like investors are buying the dip after the initial knee-jerk selloff," said Charu Chanana, chief investment strategist at Saxo. "The blue sweep hasn't changed, but markets may be recognising that political gridlock doesn't necessarily mean weaker corporate earnings."
In Asia, the bulk of selling was in AI stocks, with chipmakers Samsung, SK Hynix and TSMC sliding ​sharply ​before cutting losses. The KOSPI was last slightly higher after dropping 3% earlier.
George Efstathopoulos, portfolio manager ​and co-head of multi-asset research at Fidelity International, said he had ‌reduced overall equity exposure and dialled up exposure in defensive sectors like utilities, but thinks now is a good time to gradually rotate back into tech.
"The midterms are a clearing event that can allow investors to focus on sectors where fundamentals and pricing have diverged. Technology is one of them."
INVESTORS RUSH FOR SAFETY OF BONDS
Treasuries rallied as investors expect gridlock in Washington to cut government spending. AI regulation could also slow growth and reduce the need for rate hikes.
The yield on the benchmark US 10-year Treasury note fell 6 basis points to 4.906%, pushing the dollar sharply lower. [FRX/] [US/]
"Bonds are coming out as the clear winner as markets put the AI trade on the chopping block ‌and embrace the higher possibility that further tax cuts are put on ice and government spending ​slows," said TD Securities' Newnaha.
Kim Seok-hwan, an analyst at Mirae Asset Securities, said the Democrats' victory in ​Texas is likely to weigh on chip stocks, raising fears of tighter ​curbs on AI data-centre development in one of the fastest-growing markets for computing infrastructure in the US.
"If Texas declares a moratorium on data ‌centres, as New York did, projects could face further delays," Kim ​said. "Today's market reaction is clearly reflecting concerns ​and uncertainty over these issues."
In currencies, the dollar slid broadly against major peers. The euro rose 0.5% to $1.1249, while sterling firmed 0.37% to $1.3464. That left the dollar index 0.37% lower at 101.34. [FRX/]
The yen and the Swiss franc — both safe-haven currencies — notched up the biggest gains. The yen was 0.7% stronger at 157.55 ​per US dollar, while the Swiss franc firmed almost 0.8% ‌to 0.8144 per US dollar.
In the oil market, prices were choppy on Wednesday after sliding to a four-week low in the previous session as ​investors weighed talks to end the wars in Ukraine and Iran against worries that recent attacks in both conflicts could further disrupt supplies. [O/R]
(Reporting by ​Ankur Banerjee and Rae Wee in Singapore; Editing by Shri Navaratnam and Christopher Cushing)

articles.title_orig: Democrats seize Congress in sweeping midterm repudiation of Trump
articles.title_zh: Democrats seize Congress in sweeping midterm repudiation of Trump
articles.content_orig:
Xi urges diplomacy on Iran as Oman’s sultan makes historic visit to China
Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia – Across the Asia-Pacific region, governments and businesses reeling from the energy shock of the United States and Israel’s war on Iran are watching Tuesday’s US midterm elections closely.
Many want to see “enormous changes” during the rest of President Donald Trump’s term, analysts say, from the war on Iran to his policies on trade and tariffs. But few expect that to happen, even with the Democrats poised to take the House of Representatives, and potentially the Senate, from Trump’s Republican Party.
“Of course, everybody is watching,” said Steven Okun, a trade specialist and the chief executive of APAC Advisors, a Singapore-based consulting firm. “It’s great political theatre.”
Outside the Middle East, no region has been hit harder by the war on Iran than the Asia-Pacific. Before the start of the conflict in January, the region took in most of the Gulf oil and gas that passed through the Strait of Hormuz.
When Iran closed the chokepoint in response to the US and Israel’s strikes, much of the region was left facing shortages .
The Philippines, which relies on the Gulf for more than 90 percent of its crude oil imports, has been under a national energy emergency since March. Soaring fuel costs have drained the foreign exchange reserves of the region’s poorest economies – Cambodia, Laos, Myanmar and East Timor, according to the Institute of Southeast Asian Studies (ISEAS)-Yusof Ishak Institute in Singapore. Indonesia, Malaysia, Thailand and Vietnam have also spent heavily on fuel subsidies to shield consumers, it said.
Public opinion in the US and the Asia-Pacific region remains firmly opposed to the war, but Okun said a Democratic-controlled US Congress was unlikely to force Trump to end the eight-month conflict.
“With Iran, I don’t see [a Democrat-controlled Congress] having much change at all, other than the fact that the war will be investigated and there will be oversight hearings,” Okun told Al Jazeera. “We might even see an impeachment of the secretary of defence, but it doesn’t change the overall impact of the war.”
Under the US Constitution, Congress holds the power to formally declare war, but Trump has claimed the attacks on Iran were in self-defence and has so far ignored congressional resolutions directing him to withdraw US forces from hostilities. If a Democrat-controlled Congress passes legislation restricting military operations or cutting funding for them, Trump can veto it.
Overriding a veto requires a two-thirds majority in both chambers, which Democrats are almost certain to fall short of.
On trade and tariffs, too, analysts see little room for Congress to rein in Trump.
The US president rattled global markets last year when he imposed “reciprocal” tariffs of 10 percent to 50 percent on some 90 countries, with the aim of shrinking the US trade deficit. The Asia Pacific was again hit harder than most. Some 15 countries were hit with tariffs, with Cambodia facing a 49 percent tariff and Laos 48 percent. Vietnam was slapped with 46 percent and Myanmar 45 percent.
After the Supreme Court struck down those tariffs in February, the Trump administration turned to other tools . In July, it imposed tariffs of 10 percent and 12.5 percent on goods from 60 trading partners, accusing them of failing to stop imports made with forced labour . In Asia, the list includes China, Japan, South Korea and seven Southeast Asian nations – Cambodia, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand and Vietnam.
“In some ways, the new Congress is not going to matter to the Asia Pacific because it’s not going to affect trade policy,” Okun said. “Congress cannot change that … Tariffs don’t change. The war doesn’t change.”
Still, some analysts see a narrow opening on tariffs.
Stephen Olson, a visiting fellow at the ISEAS-Yusof Ishak Institute, argued in a recent essay that a “strong rebuke of ‘Trumpism’” at the polls could embolden a pro-free-trade wing of the Republican Party that has been “intimidated into standing down during the Trump presidency”.
That, Olson wrote, offers “a glimmer of hope” for Southeast Asian countries that depend on the US market. A Democratic-controlled Congress, he said, could also push for carve-outs and exceptions that would give the region’s exporters “a modicum of relief”. But any deeper shift in US trade policy, he added, will have to wait for the 2028 presidential election.
Joshua Kurlantzick, a senior fellow for Southeast Asia and South Asia at the Council on Foreign Relations, said the region’s wish list goes beyond trade to security.
“I think nearly all of Asia would like to see enormous changes, across many domains, during the rest of Trump’s term,” he told Al Jazeera. “But I think much of the region believes this will not happen.”
Besides “more stability” in trade and tariff policy, Asia-Pacific countries “would like to feel more stable in security guarantees from the US,” he said. They would also like a “more clear, obvious US presence” in the South China Sea , where China’s claims overlap with those of five Southeast Asian nations, and in the Taiwan Strait , which separates China from Taiwan , the self-governed island Beijing claims as its territory.
Businesses will also be watching whether a major Republican loss leads to “greater GOP willingness in Congress to stand up to Trump, along with Democrats, on issues important to companies in Asia,” Kurlantzick said, including tariffs, trade policy, arms sales and “overall economic unpredictability”.
One area where analysts do expect Congress to act is on China.
The new Congress, whichever party controls it, will pass tougher restrictions on China’s access to technology, said Okun at APAC Advisors.
These include the Remote Access Security Act, which would extend export controls to remote access of US goods, software or technology and the Chip Security Act, which would require companies to verify that advanced artificial intelligence (AI) chips remain in authorised locations, to prevent diversion to foreign adversaries. It also includes the Multilateral Alignment of Technology Controls on Hardware Act, known as the MATCH Act, which would press allies to bring their controls on chipmaking equipment in line with Washington’s, to keep advanced chipmaking technology out of China’s hands.
“The next Congress is going to pass them regardless of midterms because both parties agree on them,” Okun said. “The person who is least restrictive now on China is the US president,” he added, referring to Trump’s courting of China’s President Xi Jinping.
The two men have met twice this year as ties have warmed after a bitter and costly trade war last year. To preserve the fragile trade truce, Trump has also held off approving a $14bn package of arms sales to Taiwan, which would be the largest ever for Taipei.
Some analysts meanwhile worry that a lame-duck Trump, hemmed in at home by a Democratic Congress, could turn more forcefully to foreign policy.
“We should not be surprised by continued erratic foreign policy,” said James Guild, an assistant professor at the Indonesian International Islamic University.
“The Democrats have a poor record of effectively opposing and holding Trump accountable using conventional tools of congressional oversight,” Guild said. “We will have to wait and see if they rise to the moment this time.”

Stock futures were mixed early on Wednesday as traders speculated that Democrats were headed for majority control of Congress and some key gubernatorial wins in the 2026 U.S. midterm elections .
Futures tied to the S&P 500 traded 0.21% lower, while Nasdaq-100 futures shed 0.30%. But futures tied to the Dow Jones Industrial Average moved higher, adding 29 points, or 0.06%. Futures were off their worst levels of the session.
The Democratic Party is projected to win both chambers of Congress, according to The Associated Press. The AP also projected that Texas Democratic governor candidate Gina Hinojosa is the winner over Republican incumbent Greg Abbott. Hinojosa has pledged a moratorium on data centers in the key tech hub.
Democrats securing a sizable majority in the House and Senate — the so-called blue wave scenario — would pressure the market and especially stocks related to the artificial intelligence buildout, according to some on Wall Street. Investors fear a big Democratic win could mean more restrictions on data centers nationwide. AI-linked stocks have already pulled back in recent weeks on concern about a slowing pace in data-center spending.
Big Tech shares Microsoft , Amazon and Nvidia were all trading lower in overnight trading on Robinhood.
Elon Musk's SpaceX was down 4.6% on Robinhood, while Tesla shares were down 4.1%. Data center play CoreWeave was down 3.2% in Robinhood overnight trading, while Alphabet was some 0.6% lower.
Equities "trended lower as it's looked more likely that Democrats are going to pick up the House and most likely the Senate," said Anthony Saglimbene, chief market strategist at Ameriprise Financial, Tuesday evening as futures were pulling back.
He added: "If you get some governorships that are Democratic, what does that mean for the data center buildout, which has already seen a lot of skepticism over the last couple weeks in terms of the hyperscaler capex spending?"
AMD shares initially surged double digits in post-market action after the company, a key player in the AI trade, reported third-quarter earnings and revenue that blew past analyst expectations. The stock was last 5% higher on Robinhood as stock market futures traded lower.
On the overall market, investors believe a blue wave would also be a headwind as it likely rules out any more business-friendly policies like tax breaks and possibly increases scrutiny on industries like banking.
Renewable shares like solar stocks traded higher in the post-market on speculation a Democratic majority in Congress would halt policies by President Donald Trump taken against the industry. The Invesco Solar ETF was up 3% in Robinhood trading.
President Donald Trump may have helped ease pressure on the market a bit overnight by not challenging the midterm results in an interview with the Wall Street Journal . Trump told the WSJ, "I think we'll work with the Democrats, and we'll get along very well with them."

There are a lot of California companies that moved to Texas, thinking, 'All right, we're going to get out of this blue state and go somewhere safe,' and now it's proven that it isn't," Jay Woods, Freedom Capital Markets' chief market strategist, said in an interview with CNBC.
"You want to watch a lot of these Texas companies that moved there," he stressed.
Musk said that he was going to move the headquarters of both companies to Texas from California back in 2024. Tesla shares were down more than 4% on Robinhood.
Investors were focusing on the results of the Texas gubernatorial race for clues about the AI trade because the state represents an outsized portion of data center capacity. Democratic candidate Gina Hinojosa has an early lead over Republican incumbent Greg Abbott. Hinojosa is calling for an immediate moratorium on data centers in the state and an end any tax incentives for the build-out.
"The one thing that could really end up moving stuff though would be if Abbott were to lose Texas," said Scott Ladner, chief investment officer of Horizon Investments. "Because there is a legitimate question about, where do you build these data centers?"
"Texas is a fertile ground for that. And if he were to lose, I think that fertile ground is largely barren. So, that's going to be a challenge. And so the AI trade — at least for next couple days — does hinge on does Abbott win or not," Ladner added.
Texas represents about 27% of U.S. data center gigawatts, estimates Wells Fargo.

articles.title_orig: Chinese investors stay on sidelines despite Beijing’s latest rescue push
articles.title_zh: Chinese investors stay on sidelines despite Beijing’s latest rescue push
articles.content_orig:
Leveraged traders trimmed holdings to a one-year low this week, while new stock-account openings dropped by more than 30 per cent in October
Chinese investors refrained from bets on stocks this week, even as state support unfolded after Beijing unveiled a litany of measures to shore up confidence in the world’s second-largest equity market.
Leveraged traders trimmed their holdings to a one-year low this week, while new stock-account openings dropped by more than 30 per cent in October, according to official data. The retreat in retail enthusiasm contrasted with the government ramping up efforts to prop up stocks, including liquidity injections through two monetary tools and reported suspensions of new share sales to keep a lid on supply.
The divergence illustrates investors’ unease over whether the latest bout of government interventions will drive sustained gains in stocks, which are grappling with weak domestic demand and the fallout of a rout in AI stocks in the US. Investment banks including Bank of America and Macquarie said that state intervention might stabilise sentiment, but would fall short of fuelling a fresh rally.

articles.title_orig: Oil rises on Iran war uncertainty after Trump's Republicans face election rout
articles.title_zh: Oil rises on Iran war uncertainty after Trump's Republicans face election rout
articles.content_orig:
Crude oil prices fell Tuesday for a second consecutive session, as the market hopes the U.S. and Iran will reach a diplomatic settlement to the conflict that has disrupted global energy supplies for eight months.
U.S. West Texas Intermediate futures lost 37 cents to close at $96.09 a barrel after dipping below $95 earlier in the session. Brent crude , the international benchmark, shed $1.17 to settle at $103.60.
The move lower came after rumors circulated the U.S. and Iran were making progress toward a deal.
Oil sold off more than 7% on Monday after Washington and Tehran signaled they were both open to discussions to reach a settlement. President Donald Trump told reporters Tehran wants "to make a deal and that could happen."
Qatar is continuing to mediate talks between the U.S. and Iran, the Gulf state's foreign ministry said Tuesday. A delegation from Qatar held talks in Tehran in an effort to reach an agreement that prevents further escalation in the region and ends the U.S.-Iran conflict, the foreign ministry said.
However, Iran's Foreign Ministry spokesman Emsaeil Baqaei said Tuesday that Tehran will not accept diplomacy based on coercion, according to the state-owned media outlet Islamic Republic News Agency . It was unclear where talks actual stand.
The market had been pricing in the risk of escalation after the U.S. midterm elections , as reports circulated that Washington was drafting plans for strikes on Iran. Crude prices gained more than 10% in October in response.
The situation in the Middle East remains volatile and there's still substantial risk that fighting could break out. Washington attacked Iran's Qeshm Island on Monday, U.S. officials told The Wall Street Journal, adding that the U.S. has been carrying out "limited strikes" against the country in recent weeks.
The military campaign against Iran has been kept deliberately low-profile to avoid signaling plans for a major escalation in fighting, the report said, quoting an unnamed official.
And commercial ships continue to come under attack in the Persian Gulf, Strait of Hormuz and Gulf of Oman. At least four ship attacks have been reported since the start of the month, according to the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations Centre.
Despite these attacks, the Trump administration has also been touting a possible diplomatic solution to the conflict, with Vice President JD Vance telling CNN, "The president and I both feel really good about the prospect of potentially coming to a negotiated settlement."
On Sunday, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Trump would like to resolve the Iranian war "diplomatically," and prefers not to use military force.
High oil prices have contributed substantially to inflation and high gasoline prices in the U.S., which have become a cause of concern for Trump ahead of the midterm elections.
Last week, two Federal Reserve presidents said interest rates will need to move higher to rein in inflation. Higher rates generally crimp growth and raise costs for consumers, but help to bring down inflation.
— CNBC's Priyanka Salve contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Canva Announces Layoffs, Job Changes for About 22% of Workforce
articles.title_zh: Canva Announces Layoffs, Job Changes for About 22% of Workforce
articles.content_orig:
Canva, one of Australia's best known start-ups, has announced a shake up of the business that will affect 22% of its workers, including job cuts.
In what was "without doubt the hardest moment in our thirteen-year history" co-founder and CEO Melanie Perkins said 1,271 people would either lose their jobs, be asked to relocate or change roles.
The firm's value has reportedly dropped in the past year over concerns about the impact of artificial intelligence (AI) on its business as well as the cost of incorporating the technology into its platforms.
It had been "our hardest year yet, and as we shared earlier this year, our growth has slowed for the first time in a decade," Perkins wrote to staff.
The "incredibly hard decision" meant "significant changes," Perkins said.
"For some people, this will mean changes to their roles or being asked to relocate to centralised hubs. Sadly, it will also mean saying goodbye to teammates and friends who have helped build Canva into what it is today."
The company, which has staff in 37 countries, said Sydney would become the "primary home" for more of its product teams and that as of next year hybrid workers would be expected to spend two to three days in the office.
Earlier this year two of its backers, Blackbird Ventures and Airtree, reportedly downgraded its valuation from A$60bn ($41.8bn; £31.1bn) at the end of last year to about A$49bn.
Canva also reportedly cut its own internal valuation amid soaring AI expenses related to the roll out of new products.
"New technology is transforming what people can create, how they create it, and what they expect from the products they use," Perkins said in her note on Wednesday.
Perkins, who left university at 19 to found her first venture, launched Canva in 2013.
The company offers a variety of templates and tools to help users without technical skills or a design background to create a range of professional-looking graphics and presentations, from wedding invitations to business pitch decks.

articles.title_orig: Google researchers are fighting the company to tell the world what they know about AI
articles.title_zh: Google researchers are fighting the company to tell the world what they know about AI
articles.content_orig:
Workers inside Google’s artificial-intelligence division are asking executives to release them from non-disparagement agreements so they can discuss AI’s risks in public, The Washington Post reported. The request puts a plain question in front of one of the world’s most powerful AI employers: who gets to speak when the people closest to the technology think the public deserves a warning?
The reported dispute involves employees at Google DeepMind, including staff in London. A contract reviewed by The Washington Post reportedly bars some British employees from criticizing the company for life, including after they leave Google. Two current Google DeepMind workers told the paper that the agreements restrict public communication about AI’s potential impacts.
Google has pushed back on part of the picture. The company said it updated terms for new hires to remove the post-termination portion of non-disparagement clauses. A Google spokesperson added that the company does not enforce such clauses after employees leave and provides internal channels for escalating concerns. Disclosure pressure on AI labs is rising on several fronts, and our look at what the Anthropic amended S-1 disclosed on November 2 shows how much a lab now has to tell investors. This story asks the mirror-image question: how much can its workers tell everyone else?
Don't miss new tech stories on Google
Add Shattered once in the Google app and our stories show up in your news suggestions.
Four points hold up in the reporting available to us. First, workers in Google’s AI division are asking executives for release from non-disparagement agreements. Second, the dispute concerns Google DeepMind staff, including people based in London. Third, a contract The Washington Post reviewed reportedly bars some British employees from criticizing the company for life, even after they leave. Fourth, two current DeepMind workers said the agreements limit what they can say publicly about AI’s possible impacts.
Those are the load-bearing facts. Everything else around this story, including some of the headline phrasing that has circulated, goes further than the record does. The idea that Google researchers are collectively demanding the freedom to tell the world what they know about AI is a fair summary of the mood, but it is not independently established beyond the worker requests The Washington Post described. We have no verified count of participating researchers, no list of signatories, and no named organizer.
We also have no on-record quote from a named Google DeepMind researcher in the material available for this report. That matters for how much weight readers should put on any single claim. The two current workers appear in the reporting as sources describing the agreements, not as named spokespeople for a movement. A story built on a reviewed contract and two employees is still news, but it is a narrower story than a walkout or an open letter would be.
One detail deserves attention. The workers are reported to be asking executives to release them, which is a request, not a breach. That choice signals that at least some staff want to stay inside the rules while changing them. It also suggests they see the contract language, not company culture, as the obstacle.
A non-disparagement clause is a contract term that limits what a person can say publicly about their employer. Standard versions cover false or damaging statements. Broader versions can reach honest criticism, opinions, and even neutral descriptions of internal decisions if the wording is loose enough. Companies use them to protect reputation, and employees often sign them as part of an offer letter or a separation package without reading the fine print twice.
The difference between a narrow clause and a broad one is the whole story here. A narrow clause leaves room for a worker to say that a safety process failed or that a product carries a risk the public should weigh. A broad one makes the worker think twice before saying anything at all. When the subject is AI risk, a field where insiders often know things outsiders cannot check, that chilling effect carries real cost.
The reported contract goes beyond a standard employment-period restriction. According to The Washington Post, it bars some British employees from criticizing Google for life, including after they leave. A restriction that survives employment has no natural end date. A researcher who quits after five years of safety work would stay bound in year ten, even if the technology and the risks look nothing like they did at signing.
Note the qualifier in the reporting: the reviewed contract covers some British employees, not every DeepMind worker. We do not know the exact language used across the workforce, and the reporting does not claim a single uniform clause. Any reader judging Google’s conduct should keep that gap in view.
Google answered with two statements. The company said it updated terms for new hires to remove the post-termination portion of non-disparagement clauses. A spokesperson also said Google does not enforce non-disparagement clauses after employees leave, and that the company provides internal channels for people to escalate concerns.
Both statements carry weight, and both leave questions open. Removing the post-termination portion for new hires is a concrete contract change. It tells us Google’s lawyers saw enough risk or enough pressure to rewrite the template. A non-enforcement pledge is softer. It describes what the company does today, not what the paper allows tomorrow.
That distinction explains why employees are reported to be seeking clearer legal protection through revised contract language. A worker deciding whether to speak at a conference or give a journalist a background interview does not rely on a spokesperson’s description of enforcement habits. They rely on the text they signed. If the text says one thing and the practice says another, the safest move for the individual is silence.
Internal escalation channels address a different problem. They give employees a place to raise concerns inside the company, which helps when management listens. They do nothing for a worker who has raised concerns internally, seen no change, and now wants the public to know. The workers’ request, as reported, targets that second situation.
Google’s stated fix applies to new hires. The reporting we have does not say whether current employees, or people who already left under older terms, get the same change. That gap is the center of the dispute. A policy that improves the paperwork for the next cohort leaves the people who raised the issue on the old terms.
Several questions follow, and none has a confirmed answer in the available reporting:
Each question has a simple yes or no answer that Google could publish. The company’s decision on whether to answer them will say more about its posture than the original contract language did.
News about AI labs moves fast and headlines tend to outrun facts. The table below separates what the reporting supports from what it does not, so readers can see where the evidence stops.
Two lessons come out of that table. The core facts are solid because they rest on a document the paper reviewed and on company statements. The movement framing is softer, and readers should treat it as interpretation until someone names organizers or publishes a letter.
The reported contract covers British employees, and DeepMind has a major presence in London. That puts the dispute inside a country with its own regulators, its own employment rules, and its own public conversation about AI. UK officials have been vocal about AI risk in other domains. Our earlier report on the NCSC warning that AI malware could hit UK critical infrastructure within two years shows how seriously British security agencies treat the subject.
A government that asks the public to take AI risk seriously will find it awkward when the people who build the technology say they cannot

articles.title_orig: Midterm election results 2026: Who’s winning and what’s at stake for stocks and the economy
articles.title_zh: Midterm election results 2026: Who’s winning and what’s at stake for stocks and the economy
articles.content_orig:
Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged in Please refresh your browser to be logged in
Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.
Control of the US Congress is the prize on November 3, 2026, as Democrats attempt to wrest majorities from President Donald Trump's Republicans in the midterm elections.
Voters will also choose governors in 36 of the 50 states, and nearly every state will hold elections for its state-level legislative bodies.
Ballots have been cast for weeks, with early voting underway across the country ahead of Election Day .
The midterms , held in the middle of each four-year presidential term, by definition do not involve the president himself.
But anyone tempted to dismiss this year's contests as lacking drama or importance should weigh two statistics.
More than 100 million people are expected to cast ballots in this year's midterm voting, if turnout is anything like the previous midterm in 2022.
And as of October 30, a record $11.6 billion had been spent on political advertisements for the 2025–26 election cycle.
AdImpact, which tracks the activities, said the top spending is in battleground US Senate races in Texas, Ohio and Michigan.
Campaign finance records show Elon Musk alone has spent $442 million to support Republicans.
Midterms generally attract fewer voters than the higher-profile presidential races.
For example, more than 155 million votes were cast in the 2024 presidential election.
In the House, Republicans currently hold a 218-214 majority, with two vacancies and one independent who caucuses with Republicans.
Democrats must win a net gain of four seats to take control of the chamber.
The Senate is also in play, where Republicans hold a 53-47 majority.
Democrats must net four additional seats to get control there.
Ten races, including those in Maine, Ohio, North Carolina, Iowa and Georgia, could decide the outcome.
Trump's approval of his performance is at an all-time low of 32 percent, according to a September Reuters/Ipsos poll.
Domestic issues like rising consumer prices are likely to affect the outcome of many races and could erode support for Republicans.
Evidence suggests Democrats are more enthusiastic about voting this year than Republicans.
If early voting trends continue, it could point to a Democratic win in November.
There are also signs that Latino voters who veered to Trump in 2024 might be returning to Democrats because of frustration over the economy and some of Trump's immigration enforcement tactics.
A landslide for the Democrats, however, is far from assured.
Republicans could benefit from continued skepticism toward Democrats, a Republican spending advantage in campaigns, and fears among moderate voters over some primary wins by left-wingers.
Midterm elections generally are dangerous territory for the political party that holds the White House and/or Congress.
For 2026, that means Trump and his Republicans controlling the US Senate and House of Representatives are in perilous political positions.
The midterms can be an opportunity for voters to, in effect, grade the president's performance, and possibly trigger White House course corrections if they receive low marks.
Midterm election results can also give aspiring presidential candidates hints on how to tailor their messages to voters in the next presidential campaign, which in this case will be in 2028.
Recent history shows the shockwaves a midterm election can produce.
In the 2010 midterms, during Barack Obama's Democratic presidency, Republicans scored major victories, winning 63 additional House seats amid an underperforming US economy and weak support for Obama's landmark healthcare reform legislation.
Democrats lost their majority.
In the Senate, they held onto control despite losing six seats.
The Republican wave was a "shellacking," Obama lamented at the time.
He subsequently faced Republican demands for significant reductions to non-defense spending.
Democrats returned the favor in 2018, with Trump in the White House.
They gained a net 40 House seats but lost a net two Senate seats.
At the state level, Republicans currently control 55% of state legislative seats across the country, while Democrats hold 43.8%, according to Ballotpedia.
If Democrats manage to win the House, the next speaker — second in line for the presidency after the vice president — is likely to be Democratic Representative Hakeem Jeffries of New York.
He is currently the House Democratic leader.
Jeffries, who would become the first Black American to hold the powerful office, would be in a position to direct House committees to investigate a range of controversial activities by Trump and his associates.
Jeffries has repeatedly said Democrats would look into what he has called "unprecedented levels of corruption" during the Trump administration.
Jeffries also would steer Democrats' legislative priorities through the House.
He has said Democrats would focus on making healthcare, groceries, housing, energy and other costs more affordable.
A Republican win, on the other hand, would ensure that the speaker's gavel remains in that party's hands, either with current speaker Mike Johnson or whichever Republican prevails if he is challenged for the job.
Republican priorities are likely to be focused on additional tax cuts, huge increases in defense spending, and deeper social safety net reductions, building on Trump's 2025 "One Big Beautiful Bill."
Among the most-watched House races are Republican Representative Mike Lawler's bid for reelection to a New York district that Democratic candidate Kamala Harris won in her 2024 presidential campaign.
An open seat in a Nebraska swing district, where farmers and truckers face sharply higher fuel prices as a result of the US war against Iran, is also drawing attention.
Also high on Democrats' list of House seats they hope to take from Republicans are two in Pennsylvania and one in New Jersey.
Hovering over all of this are questions over whether Trump will try to meddle in the elections, which are administered by the 50 individual states.
Since 2020, he has repeatedly insisted there is widespread cheating in US elections, despite a lack of evidence.
State election officials and Democrats in Congress have been preparing for possible legal challenges to any moves by his administration to try to intervene.
There is no set time for when the world will learn the results of the US midterm elections.
In tight races, winners may not be called for days or even weeks.
The first individual race calls are expected to start after polls begin to close in the United States on Tuesday night, first with Indiana and Kentucky at 6 p.m. (ET) (2300 GMT).
Polls then close in Georgia, South Carolina, Vermont and Virginia at 7 p.m. (0000 GMT on November 4).
The last polls to close are in far western Alaska at 1 a.m. ET.
